cards.q: In Van Gend en Loos (1963), the Dutch transport company Van Gend en Loos was charged an increased customs duty (from 3% to 8%) on urea-formaldehyde imported from Germany, contrary to the standstill clause in Article 12 EEC (today Article 30 TFEU). The Dutch and Belgian governments argued that only the Commission or another Member State could enforce the Treaty, through the infringement procedure. What were the Court's main arguments for direct effect, and why did it reject the governments' objection? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Court derived direct effect from the spirit, general scheme and wording of the Treaty, calling the Community a "new legal order" whose subjects include individuals, and it held that the infringement procedure does not stop individuals from enforcing EU law before national courts.
• Spirit: a common market directly concerns individuals, so the Treaty is more than an agreement creating mutual obligations between states. Evidence: the preamble speaks of "peoples", the institutions exercise sovereign rights that affect citizens, and nationals take part through the European Parliament and the Economic and Social Committee.
• General scheme: the preliminary reference (then Art 177 EEC, now Art 267 TFEU) exists to secure uniform interpretation by NATIONAL courts. That only makes sense if the states accepted that nationals can invoke EU law before those courts.
• New legal order: the states limited their sovereign rights, albeit in limited fields. Its subjects are both the states and their nationals. EU law confers rights that become part of individuals' legal heritage, not only where expressly granted but also through obligations imposed in a clearly defined way on states, institutions or individuals.
• Wording: Art 12 was a clear and unconditional prohibition. It was a negative obligation (standstill), with no reservation making it depend on national implementing measures, so it was ideally suited to produce direct effects.
• Objection rejected: Arts 169/170 EEC (now Arts 258/259 TFEU) do not exclude individual enforcement. The vigilance of individuals protecting their rights gives effective supervision in addition to that of the Commission and the Member States. Result: Van Gend could rely on Art 12 before the Dutch Tariefcommissie.
Codex: Art 30 TFEU (ex Art 12 EEC), Art 267 TFEU, Arts 258–259 TFEU · Case law (not in codex): Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Costa v ENEL (6/64).

cards.q: What is meant by the "autonomy" of Union law, and how does the Court of Justice justify and protect it? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Autonomy means that EU law is an independent legal order, separate from both public international law and national law. Its validity, meaning and effects are decided only by EU law itself, and in the last resort by the CJEU.
• Origin: Van Gend en Loos ("new legal order") and Costa v ENEL (6/64): the Treaty created "its own legal system", an independent source of law that domestic provisions cannot override, however they are framed.
• Internal side: EU acts cannot be measured against national law, even constitutional law (Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70). EU concepts are interpreted autonomously and uniformly (e.g. "worker", "court or tribunal"). Primacy and direct effect follow from this.
• External side: the CJEU alone gives the final interpretation of EU law (Art 19(1) TEU, Art 267 TFEU). Member States may not submit disputes about EU law to other fora (Art 344 TFEU; Mox Plant C-459/03; Achmea C-284/16). International agreements must not undermine this (Kadi C-402/05 P; Opinion 2/13 on ECHR accession).
• Correction of a common answer: the Commission's monopoly of initiative is a feature of the Union method, not a definition of autonomy.
Codex: Art 19(1) TEU, Arts 267, 344 TFEU · Cases: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Costa v ENEL (6/64), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70), Achmea (C-284/16), Opinion 2/13.

cards.q: What are the conditions for direct effect of Union law? Do they depend on the kind of legal act and on the relationship in which the provision is invoked (vertical/horizontal)? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A provision is directly effective if it is sufficiently clear and precise and unconditional (and so capable of conferring rights). Whether it can actually be invoked also depends on the category of act and on the relationship.
• Step 1, general conditions (Van Gend en Loos): (1) sufficiently clear and precise, so that the beneficiary, the obliged party and the content can be identified; (2) unconditional, meaning no reservation making it depend on further measures by EU institutions or Member States that involve discretion. A derogation subject to judicial review does not remove this (Van Duyn, 41/74). (3) The right or obligation must be justiciable for individuals.
• Step 2, category of act: Treaty provisions and regulations (Art 288(2) TFEU): yes. Decisions (Art 288(4)): yes, even when addressed to a Member State (Grad, 9/70). Directives (Art 288(3)): as a rule NO. The exception is vertical effect after the deadline where implementation is faulty (Ratti, 148/78).
• Step 3, relationship: vertical (against the state) is the normal case. Horizontal only where the norm also binds private parties: Arts 101/102 (BRT v SABAM), Art 157 (Defrenne II), Art 45 (Angonese), regulations (Muñoz). NEVER for directives (Marshall I, Faccini Dori). No inverse vertical effect of a directive against an individual (Kolpinghuis).
Codex: Art 288 TFEU · Cases: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Van Duyn (41/74), Grad (9/70), Ratti (148/78), Marshall I (152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Kolpinghuis (80/86).

cards.q: A new EU regulation lays down detailed rules on the labelling of honey. The parliament of Member State Veridia wants to re-enact its full text as a national statute "for the sake of clarity". Can a regulation nevertheless be transposed into national law? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. A regulation is directly applicable (Art 288(2) TFEU) and must not be transposed. National re-enactment that obscures its EU nature is itself a breach of EU law. Only accompanying measures that the regulation requires or allows are permitted.
• Art 288(2): general application, binding in its entirety, directly applicable in all Member States. It becomes part of national law automatically when it enters into force (Art 297(1): publication in the OJ, entry into force on the date specified or on the 20th day).
• Ban on transposition (Variola 34/73; Commission v Italy 39/72): Member States may not adopt measures that hide the Union nature of the rule, change its content or change its date of entry into force. That would endanger uniform application and the CJEU's jurisdiction under Art 267.
• But implementing measures are needed where the regulation leaves gaps, e.g. designating authorities or setting penalties (Art 291(1) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU). They must not contradict the regulation.
• Application: Veridia may not re-enact the regulation. It may only adopt accompanying rules (competent authority, sanctions).
Codex: Arts 288(2), 291(1), 297 TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Variola (34/73), Commission v Italy (39/72).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements, say whether each is true or false, and give reasons. (a) "Only a regulation can have direct effect." (b) "Every provision of a regulation has direct effect, because regulations are directly applicable." (c) "Treaty provisions can only be invoked against Member States, never against private parties." (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: All three statements are false.
• (a) False. Direct effect is a property of individual provisions that meet the Van Gend conditions, not of a category of act. Treaty provisions (Van Gend en Loos; Reyners on Art 49), decisions (Grad, 9/70, even when addressed to a Member State) and directives (vertically, after the deadline: Van Duyn, Ratti) can be directly effective. So can general principles and Charter provisions (Kücükdeveci, Egenberger).
• (b) False. Direct applicability (Art 288(2): part of national law without transposition) is not direct effect (a provision individuals can invoke in court). A regulation provision that only obliges Member States to set up an authority, or leaves them discretion, is directly applicable but not directly effective.
• (c) False. Treaty provisions that also address private parties have horizontal direct effect: Arts 101/102 (BRT v SABAM, 127/73), equal pay in Art 157 (Defrenne II, 43/75), free movement of workers in Art 45 (Angonese, C-281/98). Only provisions addressed solely to Member States bind only the state (e.g. Art 34 as a rule).
Codex: Arts 45, 101, 102, 157, 288 TFEU · Cases: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Grad (9/70), Ratti (148/78), Defrenne II (43/75), Angonese (C-281/98), BRT v SABAM (127/73).

cards.q: Ms Duval is a flight attendant with Aeroflux, a privately owned Belgian airline. Under the airline's collective agreement, male colleagues doing identical work earn 15% more. Belgium has no specific equal-pay legislation. Ms Duval sues Aeroflux before a Belgian labour court and relies directly on Article 157 TFEU. Aeroflux replies that the Treaty binds only Member States. (a) Can Ms Duval rely on Article 157 TFEU against Aeroflux? (b) Can she claim back pay for periods long before her claim, and what did the Court decide on this point in the leading case? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes. Art 157 TFEU on equal pay has horizontal direct effect (Defrenne II). (b) Normally a ruling applies ex tunc, but in Defrenne II the Court exceptionally limited the effect in time.
• Art 157(1) TFEU: each Member State must ensure that men and women receive equal pay for equal work or work of equal value. The prohibition is addressed to Member States, but it is mandatory. At least for direct discrimination, which can be identified using only the criteria of "equal work" and "equal pay", it is clear, precise and unconditional.
• Defrenne II (43/75, 1976; a Sabena flight attendant): Art 119 EEC (now 157) applies not only to public authorities but also to collective agreements on paid labour and to contracts between individuals. It therefore has horizontal direct effect.
• Application: the collective agreement discriminates directly. The labour court must disapply the discriminatory clause (primacy) and award equal pay.
• (b) Temporal limitation: because of legal certainty (serious financial consequences, and the Member States and Commission had encouraged the belief that the provision was not directly effective), direct effect could not be relied on for pay periods before the judgment (8 April 1976). The exception was people who had already brought proceedings. Only the Court itself can impose such a limitation, and only in the judgment that gives the interpretation.
Codex: Art 157 TFEU (ex Art 119 EEC) · Case: Defrenne II (43/75).

cards.q: Roberto, an Italian who grew up in Bolzano, and Lena, an Austrian from Innsbruck, both apply for a job with a private bank in Bolzano (South Tyrol). The bank requires a certificate of bilingualism (Italian/German) that is issued only by a public authority in Bolzano after an exam held there. Lena is perfectly bilingual, as shown by her Austrian university diplomas, but she has no such certificate, and her application is rejected. (a) Can Lena rely on EU primary law against the private bank? (b) Is the requirement compatible with EU law? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes. The prohibition of nationality discrimination in Art 45 TFEU also binds private employers (Angonese). (b) The certificate requirement is indirectly discriminatory and disproportionate, so it infringes Art 45 TFEU.
• Scope: Lena is a Union citizen seeking work in another Member State, so Art 45 TFEU applies (job-seekers are covered). Art 45(2) prohibits discrimination based on nationality in employment, remuneration and other working conditions. The prohibition is clear, precise and unconditional.
• Horizontal effect: Angonese (C-281/98, 2000) held that the prohibition also applies to private persons, because it is formulated in general terms and not addressed specifically to Member States. The Court built on Walrave (36/74) and Bosman (C-415/93), which concerned collective rules.
• Restriction: the rule is neutral on nationality, but people not resident in Bolzano, mostly nationals of other Member States, have little chance of getting the certificate. This is indirect discrimination.
• Justification: requiring language skills for a job can be a legitimate aim (cf. Groener, 379/87).
• Proportionality: the requirement is not necessary, because it excludes any other proof of equivalent language skills obtained elsewhere. It is therefore disproportionate.
• Result: the requirement breaches Art 45 TFEU. Lena can rely on it before the Italian court (compensation under Italian law is possible).
Codex: Art 45(1)–(3) TFEU, Art 18 TFEU; Reg 492/2011 · Cases: Angonese (C-281/98), Walrave and Koch (36/74), Bosman (C-415/93), Groener (379/87).

cards.q: An EU regulation on marketing standards for table grapes provides that grapes may be sold under a variety name only if they meet specified quality classes. Fructa Ltd, a grape importer, finds that its competitor Vinex GmbH, a private company, sells lower-quality grapes under a premium variety name. National law gives Fructa no civil remedy, because only public authorities enforce the standards. Can Fructa sue Vinex directly in a national civil court on the basis of the regulation? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Regulations can have horizontal direct effect, and a competitor may bring civil proceedings to enforce a clear and unconditional obligation in a regulation (Muñoz, C-253/00).
• Art 288(2) TFEU: regulations are binding in their entirety and directly applicable. By their nature and their place in the system of sources, they confer rights on individuals that national courts must protect.
• Muñoz v Frumar (C-253/00, 2002; the same situation with grape marketing standards): full effectiveness of the quality rules means a trader must be able to enforce them in civil proceedings against a competitor, even where national law gives enforcement only to public authorities. Private enforcement strengthens the regulation in practice.
• Condition: the provision relied on must be clear, precise and unconditional. Quality class obligations are.
• Application: Fructa can sue Vinex, for example for an injunction. Under procedural autonomy the national court must provide an effective remedy (principle of effectiveness).
Codex: Art 288(2) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Muñoz v Frumar (C-253/00), Van Gend en Loos (26/62).

cards.q: A Council decision addressed to all Member States obliges them, from a set date, to stop levying specific national taxes on road haulage alongside the common VAT system. Germany keeps levying such a tax. Grad, a German haulage company, refuses to pay and relies on the decision before a German tax court. The tax office objects that decisions addressed to Member States cannot create rights for individuals. (a) Who is right? (b) Could Grad rely on the decision against a private competitor? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Grad is right. A decision addressed to a Member State can have vertical direct effect (Grad, 9/70). (b) No. A decision addressed to Member States binds only its addressees (Art 288(4) TFEU), so it has no horizontal effect.
• Art 288(4) TFEU: a decision is binding in its entirety, and a decision that names its addressees binds only them.
• Grad (9/70; a German road-haulage tax): it would be incompatible with the binding effect of decisions to rule out, in principle, that the persons affected can invoke the obligation. Its useful effect (effet utile) would be weakened if nationals could not rely on it in court. Whether a specific provision has direct effect depends on its nature, background and wording. Here the obligation was clear and unconditional and had a precise deadline.
• Vertical: after the deadline Germany cannot rely on its own failure, the same estoppel idea as for directives (Ratti).
• (b) A decision addressed to Member States works like a directive. It imposes obligations only on the addressee state and cannot by itself impose obligations on private parties.
Codex: Art 288(4) TFEU · Cases: Grad (9/70), Ratti (148/78).

cards.q: Mr Rossi makes solvents and varnishes in Italy. Directive A (solvents) sets labelling rules, and its transposition deadline expired two years ago. Directive B (varnishes) has a deadline that expires next year. Italy has transposed neither and still applies a stricter 1963 labelling law. Rossi labels both products according to the directives, but not according to the Italian law, and is prosecuted. (a) Can he rely on Directive A as a defence? (b) On Directive B? (c) What is the rationale? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes for the solvents. Directive A has vertical direct effect because its deadline has expired. (b) No for the varnishes. Before the deadline a directive has no direct effect. (c) The rationale is estoppel and effet utile: a defaulting state may not rely on its own failure.
• Starting rule: directives bind Member States as to the result (Art 288(3) TFEU) and as a rule have NO direct effect. Vertical direct effect is the exception.
• Conditions (Ratti, 148/78, on these facts): (1) the provision is clear, precise and unconditional (labelling rules are); (2) there is an implementation failure (no transposition, incorrect transposition, or incorrect application); (3) the deadline has expired; (4) it is relied on against the state. Here it is used as a shield in a prosecution brought by the state, which is allowed.
• (a) Directive A: all conditions are met. The Italian court must disapply the conflicting 1963 law, and Italy may not punish someone who complied with the directive.
• (b) Directive B: the deadline has not expired, so there is no direct effect and the stricter law still applies. Until the deadline the state must only refrain from seriously compromising the directive's result (Inter-Environnement Wallonie), which an old, pre-existing law does not do.
• (c) Rationale: estoppel (a Member State cannot rely on its own failure against individuals), the effet utile of Art 288(3), and the logic of Art 267 (Van Duyn 41/74; Ratti).
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Ratti (148/78), Van Duyn (41/74), Inter-Environnement Wallonie (C-129/96).

cards.q: Directive 2011/83 on consumer rights gives consumers 14 days to withdraw from contracts concluded away from business premises. State Nordalia has not transposed it, although the deadline has passed. (a) Ms Kleo signed a language-course contract at a railway station with EduPlus, a private company. She withdraws after 5 days, and EduPlus sues her for the price. (b) Ms Ria signed an identical contract at the station with the Nordalian State Language Institute, a public body, and also withdraws. Can Kleo and Ria rely on the directive? What other routes are open to Kleo? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Ria can rely on the directive against the public institute (vertical direct effect). Kleo cannot rely on it against EduPlus, because directives have no horizontal direct effect (Faccini Dori). Kleo can still use consistent interpretation and a Francovich claim against Nordalia.
• Ria: the vertical conditions are met. The withdrawal right is clear, precise and unconditional, the directive was not transposed, the deadline has expired, and the defendant is the state. Under Marshall I (152/84) the state can be sued in whatever capacity it acts, whether as authority, employer or contracting party.
• Kleo: a directive cannot by itself impose obligations on an individual, so it cannot be relied on as such against a private party (Marshall I; Faccini Dori, C-91/92, a contract signed at a railway station). Reasons: directives are addressed only to Member States (Art 288(3)); a private party has committed no default, so estoppel does not apply; the distinction from regulations would be blurred; legal certainty.
• Kleo's alternatives: (1) consistent interpretation of Nordalian contract law in the light of the directive, as far as possible and not contra legem (Von Colson, Marleasing, Pfeiffer); (2) otherwise state liability. Non-transposition is per se a sufficiently serious breach (Dillenkofer); the directive confers rights and there is a causal link, so she can claim damages from Nordalia before national courts (Francovich); (3) a complaint to the Commission leading to Art 258/260(3), which is no personal remedy.
• Faccini Dori itself pointed to Francovich as the answer to the unequal treatment of Kleo and Ria.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Marshall I (152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Marleasing (C-106/89), Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Dillenkofer (C-178/94).

cards.q: A Dutch café owner sells tap water with added carbon dioxide under the label "mineral water". A directive on natural mineral waters, whose deadline has expired, would prohibit this labelling, but it has not been correctly transposed, and Dutch law as it stands arguably does not prohibit it. The public prosecutor charges the owner and relies directly on the directive to establish criminal liability. Is that possible? And may the court interpret Dutch law in conformity with the directive? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. A Member State cannot rely on an unimplemented directive against an individual (no "inverse vertical" direct effect), and a directive can never by itself create or aggravate criminal liability. Consistent interpretation is limited by legal certainty and non-retroactivity (Kolpinghuis Nijmegen, 80/86).
• Vertical direct effect exists to protect individuals against the defaulting state (estoppel). The state cannot benefit from its own failure by using the directive against a citizen (Kolpinghuis, on these facts; confirmed in Arcaro, C-168/95).
• Criminal law: a directive cannot, by itself and independently of national implementing law, determine or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis; Berlusconi C-387/02). This reflects nullum crimen sine lege (Art 49(1) Charter).
• Consistent interpretation: courts must read national law in the light of the directive (Von Colson), but general principles of law limit this duty, in particular legal certainty and non-retroactivity. It cannot produce criminal liability that national law does not itself establish (Kolpinghuis; Pupino C-105/03).
• Result: the charge cannot rest on the directive. A conviction is possible only if existing Dutch law already covers the conduct without being stretched.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Art 49(1) Charter · Cases: Kolpinghuis Nijmegen (80/86), Arcaro (C-168/95), Berlusconi (C-387/02), Pupino (C-105/03).

cards.q: An equal-treatment directive prohibits compulsory retirement of women at an earlier age than men. Its deadline has expired, and State Tarvia has not transposed it. Three women are forced to retire at 60, while their male colleagues retire at 65. They work for: (a) Tarvian Railways plc, wholly owned by the state, which runs the national rail network under a statutory monopoly; (b) Guarantee Fund Ltd, a privately owned company with no state shareholding, which is entrusted by statute with compensating victims of uninsured drivers and may collect compulsory levies from all motor insurers; (c) a private supermarket chain. Against which employers can they rely on the directive? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) and (b) are emanations of the state, so the directive has vertical direct effect against them. (c) is a private party, so there is no direct effect and only the workarounds remain.
• Vertical conditions: the prohibition is clear, precise and unconditional (Marshall I: equal retirement age), the deadline has expired, and it has not been transposed. The only question is whether the employer counts as "the state". Under Marshall I (152/84) the state can be sued in any capacity, including as employer.
• Foster v British Gas (C-188/89): a body is an emanation of the state, whatever its legal form, if the state has made it responsible for providing a public service under state control and it has special powers beyond the normal rules between individuals.
• Farrell (C-413/15, 2017): the Foster criteria are NOT cumulative. It is enough that the body is subject to the authority or control of the state, OR that it is entrusted with a task in the public interest and has special powers for that purpose. The Irish Motor Insurers' Bureau, a private company, qualified.
• (a) State ownership plus a public service under statutory monopoly (control and special powers): emanation.
• (b) Privately owned, but entrusted by law with a public-interest task and given special powers (compulsory levies): emanation under Farrell.
• (c) No control and no public task, so a purely horizontal case with no direct effect (Faccini Dori). Remaining routes: consistent interpretation; arguably the Charter's prohibition of sex discrimination (Arts 21(1), 23 Charter, on the Mangold/Egenberger line); a Francovich claim against Tarvia.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Arts 21, 23 Charter · Cases: Marshall I (152/84), Foster v British Gas (C-188/89), Farrell (C-413/15), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: Inter-Environnement, a Belgian non-profit environmental association, asks the Belgian Conseil d'État to annul a decree of the Walloon Regional Government of 9 April 1992 on toxic and hazardous waste. It argues that the decree conflicts with Directive 91/689 on hazardous waste. Belgium issued the decree after the directive was adopted, but before its transposition period expired. The decree exempts certain waste operations from the permit requirement that the directive would impose. Can the association rely on EU law? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not on direct effect of the directive, because the deadline had not expired. But yes on the Member State's duty, derived from Art 4(3) TEU together with Art 288(3) TFEU, to refrain during the transposition period from measures liable seriously to compromise the result the directive prescribes (Inter-Environnement Wallonie, C-129/96). The Conseil d'État must assess whether the decree does so.
• No direct effect: vertical direct effect requires the deadline to have expired (Ratti), so the directive's provisions cannot yet be invoked as such.
• But the transposition period is not legally empty. Member States need not adopt measures before the deadline, and they may adopt transitional or step-by-step measures that do not yet conform. What they must not do is adopt provisions liable seriously to compromise the result prescribed (IEW, based on then Arts 5(2) and 189(3) EC). This is the EU counterpart of Art 18 VCLT.
• Criteria for the national court: whether the measure presents itself as the full and definitive transposition; the concrete effects of applying the non-conforming provisions; and how long they last, i.e. whether they will make it impossible or very difficult to reach the result in time.
• Application: a definitive decree adopted after the directive that permanently exempts operations from permits can seriously compromise the result. The Conseil d'État may then annul or disapply it, so the association can rely on EU law (the duty of abstention). The Conseil d'État referred the question under Art 267.
• Related duty: after a directive is adopted, courts must also avoid interpreting national law in a way that would seriously compromise its objective (Adeneler, C-212/04).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU, Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 267 TFEU · Cases: Inter-Environnement Wallonie (C-129/96), Ratti (148/78), Adeneler (C-212/04).

cards.q: The Spanish company Marleasing sues La Comercial, a private company. It argues that La Comercial's founding contract is void for "lack of cause" under a general provision of the Spanish Civil Code that pre-dates the directive, because La Comercial was set up to defraud creditors. La Comercial relies on the First Company Law Directive, which exhaustively lists the grounds on which a company may be declared void. "Lack of cause" is not among them. Spain had not transposed the directive, although the deadline had passed. (a) Can La Comercial rely on the directive? (b) What must the Spanish court do? (c) What are the limits? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Not through direct effect, because the dispute is horizontal. (b) The Spanish court must interpret its Civil Code, as far as possible, in conformity with the directive, so that a company cannot be declared void on grounds the directive does not list (Marleasing, C-106/89). (c) Limits: no interpretation contra legem, legal certainty and non-retroactivity, no criminal liability.
• (a) Private v private: directives have no horizontal direct effect (Marshall I, Faccini Dori).
• (b) Duty of consistent interpretation ("indirect effect"): under Von Colson (14/83), based on Art 4(3) TEU and Art 288(3) TFEU, it binds all state authorities, including courts. Marleasing: it covers national law adopted before OR after the directive and applies in disputes between private parties. The directive need not be directly effective. Pfeiffer (C-397/01): the court must consider the whole body of national law and use every interpretative method it recognises to reach the directive's result.
• (c) Limits: the duty applies only "as far as possible". It cannot justify interpreting national law contra legem (Adeneler C-212/04; Dominguez C-282/10). It is bounded by legal certainty and non-retroactivity and cannot create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis; Pupino). But a court must depart from settled national case law that is incompatible with the directive (DI, C-441/14).
• If consistent interpretation is impossible, the fallback is state liability (Francovich).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU, Art 288(3) TFEU · Cases: Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Pfeiffer (C-397/01 to C-403/01), Adeneler (C-212/04), Dominguez (C-282/10), DI (C-441/14).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements, say whether each is true or false, and give reasons. (a) "Under the doctrine of indirect effect, national courts must interpret national law contra legem in conformity with a directive if their national legal system allows it." (b) "The duty of consistent interpretation applies only to national law adopted to implement the directive." (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both statements are false.
• (a) False. The duty of consistent interpretation (Von Colson, Marleasing) is an obligation under EU law to interpret national law "as far as possible" in the light of the directive's wording and purpose, using all interpretative methods recognised by national law (Pfeiffer). It NEVER requires an interpretation contra legem (Adeneler, Dominguez). If national law is clear and cannot be reconciled with the directive, consistent interpretation ends there. Only another doctrine can then help (a general principle or Charter right, incidental effect), or else a Francovich claim.
• (b) False. It covers ALL national law, whether adopted before or after the directive (Marleasing), and it applies to EU law generally, not only to directives. It normally applies from the end of the transposition period, but even before that courts must avoid interpretations that would seriously compromise the directive's objective (Adeneler).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU, Art 288(3) TFEU · Cases: Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Pfeiffer (C-397/01), Adeneler (C-212/04), Dominguez (C-282/10).

cards.q: Italy notifies the Commission of a draft law on labelling the geographical origin of olive oil, as the technical-standards directive requires (today Directive (EU) 2015/1535, formerly Directive 83/189). Italy then adopts the law before the mandatory standstill period has ended. Unilever delivers olive oil to the Italian retailer Central Food, labelled in line with EU law but not with the new Italian law. Central Food refuses to pay, relying on the Italian law. Can Unilever rely on the directive in this contractual dispute between private parties? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. A technical regulation adopted in breach of the notification or standstill obligations is inapplicable, and this can be invoked even in a dispute between private parties. This is the "incidental horizontal effect" of directives (CIA Security C-194/94; Unilever C-443/98).
• The directive imposes procedural duties on the STATE: notification and standstill. A breach is a substantial procedural defect that makes the national technical rule inapplicable (CIA Security, unfair-competition proceedings between competitors).
• Unilever: the same applies in contractual proceedings between private parties. The directive creates no rights or obligations for individuals and does not define the substance of the legal rule the court applies. It only removes the national rule. That is why the ban on horizontal direct effect (Faccini Dori) is not breached.
• Application: the Italian court must disapply the Italian labelling law. The contract is governed by the remaining national law, so Central Food must pay for the oil.
• Assessment: in practice the private party (Central Food) loses out. Incidental effect is a workaround, not a formal exception.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Directive (EU) 2015/1535, Arts 5–6 · Cases: CIA Security (C-194/94), Unilever Italia (C-443/98), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: UK authorities renewed an old mining permission for Conygar Quarry, which is privately operated, without the environmental impact assessment (EIA) that the EIA Directive requires. The deadline had expired, and the directive had not been correctly applied. Mrs Wells, a neighbour, sues the Secretary of State and asks the court to revoke or suspend the permission. The quarry owners argue that this would impose obligations on them under a directive, which EU law does not allow. Can Mrs Wells rely on the directive? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. She invokes the directive vertically against the state, and the adverse consequences for the quarry owners are merely incidental, so they do not bar reliance (Delena Wells, C-201/02).
• Vertical: the EIA obligation is addressed to the competent authority, is sufficiently clear and unconditional, and its deadline has expired. The defendant is the Secretary of State.
• Wells: "mere adverse repercussions on the rights of third parties, even if the repercussions are certain", do not justify preventing an individual from invoking a directive against the state. The duty to carry out an EIA is not directly linked to any obligation the directive places on the quarry owners.
• Distinguish two situations that remain excluded: inverse vertical effect (the state invokes the directive against an individual, Kolpinghuis) and horizontal effect (a directive imposes its obligations on a private party, Faccini Dori).
• Consequence: the state must remedy the failure, e.g. by revoking or suspending the permission and carrying out an EIA, or by paying compensation. How it does so falls under procedural autonomy, within the limits of equivalence and effectiveness.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Delena Wells (C-201/02), Kolpinghuis (80/86), Faccini Dori (C-91/92).

cards.q: Ms Kücükdeveci worked for Swedex, a private company, from the age of 18. When she was dismissed at 28, after 10 years' service, her notice period was calculated as if she had only 3 years' service, because § 622 of the German Civil Code (BGB) disregards employment before the age of 25. Directive 2000/78 on equal treatment in employment prohibits age discrimination, and its deadline has expired. German courts cannot interpret § 622 BGB any other way, because its wording is unambiguous. (a) Can she rely on EU law against Swedex? (b) Must the German court first make a preliminary reference? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes, though not on the directive as such (no horizontal direct effect). She can rely on the general principle of EU law prohibiting age discrimination, to which Directive 2000/78 gives concrete expression. The court must disapply § 622 BGB (Kücükdeveci, C-555/07, following Mangold, C-144/04). (b) No. A reference is optional unless the court decides at last instance.
• The directive route is blocked: the employer is private, and consistent interpretation would be contra legem.
• General principle: Mangold (C-144/04, 2005) held that non-discrimination on grounds of age is a general principle of EU law, drawn from international instruments and the Member States' common constitutional traditions. Today it is also in Art 21(1) Charter. Kücükdeveci: the directive merely gives the principle specific expression. Because the situation falls within the scope of EU law (the deadline has expired and a dismissal is a condition of employment), the principle applies. The national court must give it full effect and disapply any contrary national provision, even between private parties.
• Discrimination: unequal treatment directly based on age, and not justified. The stated aim, giving employers flexibility with young workers, is not served, because the rule applies to everyone who joined before 25, whatever their age when dismissed.
• (b) The court may, but need not, refer before disapplying (Art 267(2)), whatever national rules say. A court of last instance must refer if it has doubts (Art 267(3)).
• Later developments: DI (C-441/14): settled national case law to the contrary must be abandoned. Egenberger (C-414/16): Art 21 Charter itself confers a right that can be invoked between private parties.
Codex: Art 6(3) TEU, Arts 21(1), 51(1) Charter, Art 267 TFEU; Directive 2000/78 · Cases: Mangold (C-144/04), Kücükdeveci (C-555/07), DI (C-441/14), Egenberger (C-414/16).

cards.q: A and B applied for an allowance in lieu of the paid annual leave their husbands had not taken before they died. A's husband worked for a municipality (public sector). B's husband worked for a private company. German law, as consistently interpreted by the Federal Labour Court, excluded such claims by spouses of deceased workers, because the leave entitlement was deemed to lapse on death. Article 7 of the Working Time Directive 2003/88 guarantees at least four weeks' paid annual leave. Can both A and B rely on Article 31(2) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, both can. The right to paid annual leave in Art 31(2) Charter is mandatory and unconditional and can be invoked against a public and a private employer alike. A can additionally rely on Art 7 of Directive 2003/88 (vertically). B can rely only on the Charter (Bauer and Willmeroth, C-569/16 and C-570/16, 2018).
• Scope (Art 51(1) Charter): the Charter applies because the situation is governed by EU law, namely Art 7 of Directive 2003/88 (Åkerberg Fransson). The allowance in lieu is an integral part of the right to paid leave. It does not lapse on death and passes to the heirs.
• First step: try to interpret German law consistently. If that is impossible because of settled case law excluding the claim, move on.
• A (the municipality is part of the state): Art 7 of the directive is unconditional and sufficiently precise, so it has vertical direct effect after the deadline. Art 31(2) Charter applies as well. The court must disapply the national rule.
• B (private employer): the directive has no horizontal effect (Faccini Dori). But the right in Art 31(2) Charter is an essential principle of EU social law. It is mandatory and unconditional and needs no concretisation by EU or national law. Art 51(1) does not rule out that private parties are directly bound. The court must disapply the national rule, so B's claim succeeds.
• This is a primary-law workaround on the Mangold/Egenberger logic. Limit: the Charter provision must be sufficient in itself to confer a right. Art 27 Charter, for example, is not (AMS, C-176/12).
Codex: Art 6(1) TEU, Arts 31(2), 51(1), 52(5) Charter, Art 288(3) TFEU; Directive 2003/88, Art 7 · Cases: Bauer and Willmeroth (C-569/16 and C-570/16), Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10), Egenberger (C-414/16), AMS (C-176/12).

cards.q: Can an individual claim damages from a Member State for a breach of EU law? On what legal basis, under which conditions, and before which court? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. State liability is a principle inherent in the system of the Treaties (Francovich). Its conditions are set by EU law (Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III): a rule intended to confer rights, a sufficiently serious breach and a direct causal link to the damage. The claim is brought before national courts under national procedure.
• Basis: an unwritten general principle of EU law, derived from the full effectiveness of EU law and the protection of individual rights (Francovich, C-6/90 and C-9/90), the duty of sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU) and today Art 19(1)(2) TEU. It is NOT Art 340(2) TFEU, which concerns only the Union's liability, although Brasserie drew on the principles behind that article to align the conditions.
• Conditions (Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III, C-46/93 and C-48/93): (1) the rule infringed is intended to confer rights on individuals; (2) the breach is sufficiently serious, i.e. the Member State manifestly and gravely disregarded the limits of its discretion; (3) there is a direct causal link between the breach and the damage. Francovich's version for non-transposition of a directive (the result involves rights for individuals, their content is identifiable from the directive, causal link) is the same in substance (Dillenkofer).
• Any organ of the state can cause liability: the legislature (Brasserie), the administration (Hedley Lomas), a court of last instance (Köbler).
• Direct effect is not required, and no fault is required beyond a sufficiently serious breach. Compensation must match the loss, including lost profit.
• Procedure: before national courts under national rules (procedural autonomy), subject to equivalence and effectiveness. National law may ask whether the injured person showed reasonable diligence, e.g. by using available remedies in time.
Codex: Arts 4(3), 19(1) TEU; compare Art 340(2) TFEU · Cases: Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III (C-46/93 and C-48/93), Dillenkofer (C-178/94), Köbler (C-224/01).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements, say whether each is true or false, and give reasons. (a) "A claim for damages against a Member State for breach of Union law can be based on Article 340(2) TFEU." (b) "With a Francovich state liability claim, one can assert breaches of EU law committed by EU institutions." (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both are false. Art 340(2) TFEU and Francovich concern different defendants: the Union on the one hand, the Member States on the other.
• (a) False. Art 340(2) TFEU governs the non-contractual liability of the UNION for damage caused by its institutions or servants. Such actions go to the General Court (Arts 268 and 256(1) TFEU). A Member State's liability is an unwritten general principle of EU law (Francovich), enforced before national courts. The two are linked in substance: Brasserie and Bergaderm (C-352/98 P) aligned the conditions.
• (b) False. Francovich liability is directed against the Member State (its legislature, administration or courts). For breaches by EU institutions the route is an action for damages under Arts 268 and 340(2) TFEU. Conditions: a sufficiently serious breach of a rule conferring rights on individuals, damage, and a causal link (Bergaderm). The limitation period is 5 years (Art 46 Statute).
Codex: Arts 256(1), 268, 340(2) TFEU; Art 46 Statute of the CJEU · Cases: Francovich (C-6/90), Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93), Bergaderm (C-352/98 P).

cards.q: Two directives, both with expired deadlines. (a) State Arkos simply did not transpose the Package Travel Directive, which requires tour organisers to provide security for refunds in case of insolvency. Tourists lose their prepayments when their tour operator goes bankrupt. (b) State Belmar transposed a telecommunications directive, but it read one ambiguous provision in a reasonable way, as several other Member States also did. The Court of Justice later rejected that reading, and the operator TelCo suffered losses. Is each breach "sufficiently serious" for state liability? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes. Failing entirely to transpose within the deadline is per se a sufficiently serious breach (Dillenkofer). (b) Probably not. An excusable, good-faith misreading of an unclear provision is not a manifest and grave disregard of discretion (British Telecommunications).
• Test (Brasserie): did the Member State manifestly and gravely disregard the limits of its discretion? Factors: how clear and precise the rule is; how much discretion it leaves; whether the breach and the damage were intentional; whether any error of law was excusable; whether a position taken by an EU institution contributed; whether measures contrary to EU law were adopted or kept. A breach is always serious if it continued despite a judgment finding the infringement, a preliminary ruling, or settled case law showing the conduct was unlawful.
• Where discretion is considerably reduced or non-existent, a mere infringement can be enough (Hedley Lomas, C-5/94).
• (a) Arkos had no discretion about whether to transpose by the deadline, so the breach is per se sufficiently serious (Dillenkofer, C-178/94 and others, package travel). The directive confers rights (refund security for travellers) with identifiable content, and there is a causal link, so Arkos is liable.
• (b) The provision was imprecise and reasonably open to Belmar's good-faith reading, which other Member States shared, and there was no guidance from case law or the Commission. So the breach is not sufficiently serious (British Telecommunications, C-392/93) and there is no liability. The national court applies the criteria, but the CJEU may already give the answer.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III (C-46/93 and C-48/93), Hedley Lomas (C-5/94), Dillenkofer (C-178/94), British Telecommunications (C-392/93).

cards.q: Professor Köbler, a German national, had taught for many years at universities in several Member States before becoming a professor in Vienna. Austrian law granted a special length-of-service increment only for service at Austrian universities. The Austrian Verwaltungsgerichtshof, deciding at last instance, withdrew its preliminary reference and rejected his claim, misreading a CJEU judgment. Köbler now sues Austria for damages. (a) Can a Member State be liable for a judgment of its highest court? (b) Under which conditions? (c) Does res judicata stand in the way? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes (Köbler, C-224/01). (b) The Brasserie conditions apply, but a breach by a court of last instance must be "manifest". (c) No. The damages claim does not reopen the judgment.
• (a) State liability covers all organs of the state, including the courts. Courts of last instance are decisive for protecting EU rights because their errors can no longer be corrected, and the state is treated as a single entity.
• (b) Conditions: a rule conferring rights (Art 45 TFEU, because the increment obstructed free movement of workers); a sufficiently serious breach, which for a last-instance court exists only in the exceptional case where it manifestly infringed the applicable law; and a causal link. Relevant factors: the clarity and precision of the rule, whether the infringement was intentional, whether the error of law was excusable, the position taken by any EU institution, and non-compliance with the duty to refer under Art 267(3). A breach is in any event manifest if the judgment clearly disregards CJEU case law.
• (c) The damages action is against the state and does not seek to revise the judgment, so res judicata is no obstacle.
• Outcome in Köbler: Art 45 was infringed, but not manifestly, because the point was not clearly settled. National law may not exclude liability for the interpretation of law or the assessment of facts, nor limit it to intent or gross negligence where that goes beyond the "manifest" test (Traghetti del Mediterraneo, C-173/03).
Codex: Art 45 TFEU, Art 267(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Köbler (C-224/01), Traghetti del Mediterraneo (C-173/03), Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93).

cards.q: What is meant by the principle of procedural autonomy? What are its limits? Illustrate with a national time limit for reclaiming charges levied in breach of EU law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Where there are no EU procedural rules, each Member State designates the competent courts and lays down the procedure for enforcing EU rights. This autonomy is limited by the principles of equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe, Comet).
• Background: enforcement is decentralised. National courts protect EU rights (Art 19(1)(2) TEU; Art 4(3) TEU). First check whether EU procedural rules exist, e.g. GDPR Arts 77 ff. or Directive 2014/104. If they do, they prevail.
• Rewe (33/76) and Comet (45/76): national time limits for reclaiming charges levied contrary to EU law are acceptable in the interest of legal certainty, provided that (1) equivalence: the conditions are no less favourable than for similar domestic actions; and (2) effectiveness: they do not make it impossible in practice to exercise EU rights. The modern formula is "practically impossible or excessively difficult" (Impact, C-268/06). A reasonable time limit that applies equally to domestic claims passes. A two-week limit would fail effectiveness even if it applied equally.
• Beyond this, effective judicial protection (Art 19(1) TEU, Art 47 Charter) may require remedies that national law lacks: interim relief (Factortame I), damages (Francovich), disapplication (Simmenthal).
• Correction of a common error: procedural autonomy does NOT govern preliminary references. The right and duty to refer follow from Art 267 TFEU itself, not from national procedure.
Codex: Arts 4(3), 19(1)(2) TEU, Art 47 Charter · Cases: Rewe (33/76), Comet (45/76), Impact (C-268/06), Factortame I (C-213/89).

cards.q: The Irish Merchant Shipping Act 2020 introduced new nationality and residence requirements for registering fishing vessels as Irish. Spanish-owned fishing companies were then barred from fishing in Irish waters. They sought judicial review of the Act's compatibility with the EU Treaties (freedom of establishment) and asked for interim relief suspending the Act until final judgment. Under Irish common law, courts cannot suspend Acts of Parliament by way of interim relief. Can the fishers rely on EU law to obtain interim relief? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. In a case governed by EU law, a national court that considers the only obstacle to granting interim relief to be a rule of national law must set that rule aside (Factortame I, C-213/89).
• The facts mirror Factortame I (UK Merchant Shipping Act 1988; reference from the House of Lords).
• Reasoning: primacy and Simmenthal (106/77). Every national court must set aside any national legislative, administrative or judicial rule or practice that would impair the full effectiveness of EU law. It would be impaired if a national rule could stop a court from granting interim relief to secure the effectiveness of the final judgment on the rights claimed under EU law. Art 4(3) TEU and today Art 19(1)(2) TEU and Art 47 Charter support this.
• Application: the Irish court must disapply the common-law bar. Whether relief is actually granted then depends on the ordinary conditions for interim relief (e.g. a serious case, urgency, balance of interests), which must respect equivalence and effectiveness. The court may refer the substantive question under Art 267. In Factortame II (C-221/89) the nationality requirements were held contrary to what is now Art 49 TFEU.
• Follow-up: damages for the loss suffered are available under Factortame III, applying the Brasserie conditions.
Codex: Arts 4(3), 19(1)(2) TEU, Art 49 TFEU, Art 47 Charter · Cases: Factortame I (C-213/89), Simmenthal (106/77), Factortame II (C-221/89), Brasserie du Pêcheur/Factortame III (C-46/93 and C-48/93).

cards.q: (a) An Italian first-instance judge finds that a statute passed after an EU regulation conflicts with it. Under Italian constitutional law as then understood, only the Constitutional Court could set a statute aside. Must the judge wait for the Constitutional Court? (b) Variant: Austrian law requires ordinary courts that consider a statute contrary to the Charter to ask the Verfassungsgerichtshof to annul it with general effect. Is such a priority procedure compatible with EU law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No. Every national court must itself set aside conflicting national law immediately, whether it came before or after the EU rule, without waiting for repeal by legislative or constitutional means (Simmenthal, 106/77). (b) Only if the ordinary courts remain free to refer to the CJEU at any stage, to grant interim protection, and to disapply the statute after the constitutional proceedings (A v B, C-112/13).
• Simmenthal: directly applicable EU rules must be applied fully and uniformly from their entry into force. A national court must apply EU law in its entirety and set aside, of its own motion, any conflicting national provision. Any rule or practice that withholds this power from the court, even temporarily, is incompatible with the very essence of EU law.
• Primacy means disapplication, not nullity. The national rule remains valid outside the scope of EU law (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97).
• (b) A v B (C-112/13, 2014, Austria), following Melki and Abdeli (C-188/10): a priority constitutional review is compatible with EU law only if the ordinary courts remain free (i) to refer to the CJEU at any stage, even after the constitutional proceedings; (ii) to adopt any measure needed for interim judicial protection; and (iii) to disapply the statute afterwards if they consider it contrary to EU law.
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU, Art 267 TFEU · Cases: Simmenthal (106/77), IN.CO.GE.'90 (C-10/97), Melki and Abdeli (C-188/10 and C-189/10), A v B (C-112/13).

cards.q: What constitutes the principle of decentralised enforcement of EU law? Give examples of direct enforcement by the Union itself, and comment on this statement: "The Commission can, contrary to the principle that enforcement of Union law is the responsibility of the Member States, directly enforce Union law itself." (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: As a rule, EU law is enforced by the Member States (decentralised or indirect enforcement). Direct enforcement by EU bodies is the exception and needs an explicit legal basis. The statement is therefore true, but only within those exceptions.
• Decentralised enforcement: Member State authorities implement EU law (Art 291(1) TFEU: Member States adopt all national measures needed to implement binding Union acts). National courts protect EU rights (Art 19(1)(2) TEU), under procedural autonomy limited by equivalence and effectiveness, and subject to the duty of sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU). Art 267 links national courts to the CJEU.
• Examples of direct enforcement, each with an explicit basis: competition law, where the Commission investigates, prohibits and fines undertakings (Art 105 TFEU; Reg 1/2003, Arts 7, 17–24); state aid control and recovery decisions (Art 108 TFEU; Reg 2015/1589); the Digital Markets Act; trade defence, e.g. anti-dumping duties imposed by Commission regulation; management of Union funds and research funding; EU staff matters; and ECB supervision of significant banks (SSM).
• Corrections of common errors: an exclusive competence (Art 3 TFEU, e.g. the customs union) is not the same as direct enforcement. Customs duties are collected by NATIONAL customs authorities under the Union Customs Code. A citizen's complaint to the Commission leads to supervision of the Member State (Art 258), not to direct enforcement against individuals.
• Even competition law is largely decentralised since Reg 1/2003: national competition authorities and courts apply Arts 101 and 102 in full (Arts 5, 6 Reg 1/2003).
Codex: Art 291(1) TFEU, Arts 4(3), 19(1) TEU, Arts 105, 108 TFEU; Reg 1/2003, Arts 4–7, 23 · Case: Rewe (33/76).

cards.q: Directive X gives temporary agency workers the right to equal pay with the user company's permanent staff. Its deadline has expired, and State Mirania has not transposed it. Tomas, an agency worker, is paid 30% less than permanent staff at Autofab, a private car factory in which the state holds 10% of the shares without any special rights. Mirania's Labour Code contains a general clause requiring "fair remuneration". Advise Tomas: which routes can he use to obtain equal pay or compensation, and in which order? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: There is no direct effect against Autofab, which is private and not an emanation of the state. Tomas should first argue consistent interpretation of the "fair remuneration" clause, then check the general-principle/Charter route, and otherwise claim damages from Mirania under Francovich.
• Step 1, direct effect: the provision is clear, precise and unconditional, the deadline has expired and there is no transposition, but the relationship is horizontal. Directives have no horizontal direct effect (Marshall I, Faccini Dori).
• Step 2, emanation of the state? A 10% shareholding without control or special powers, and no task in the public interest, does not make Autofab an emanation (Foster, Farrell).
• Step 3, consistent interpretation: the open clause "fair remuneration" can be read in line with the directive's equal-pay rule without any contra legem problem. The court must use every recognised method of interpretation (Von Colson, Marleasing, Pfeiffer). This is the strongest route.
• Step 4, incidental or triangular effect: not relevant, because no state measure is being challenged.
• Step 5, general principle or Charter: this helps only if a primary-law right that is sufficient in itself covers the claim (Mangold, Egenberger, Bauer). Equal pay for agency workers is not clearly such a right, and the general equality clause (Art 20 Charter) is doubtful here.
• Step 6, state liability: the rule confers rights; non-transposition is per se sufficiently serious (Dillenkofer); the pay difference is the damage; the causal link exists. Tomas can claim from Mirania before national courts (Francovich).
• In addition, a complaint to the Commission can lead to Art 258/260(3), but that gives Tomas no personal remedy.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU, Arts 20, 51 Charter · Cases: Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Foster (C-188/89), Farrell (C-413/15), Marleasing (C-106/89), Pfeiffer (C-397/01), Mangold (C-144/04), Francovich (C-6/90), Dillenkofer (C-178/94).

cards.q: The Austrian Supreme Court (OGH), deciding at last instance, rejects a claim that turns on a disputed interpretation of an EU regulation. It makes no preliminary reference, although the Court of Justice has never decided the question and courts in other Member States interpret the provision differently. The losing party asks what the consequences of this breach of the obligation to refer are, under EU law and under Austrian law. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The OGH breached Art 267(3) TFEU. Possible consequences are infringement proceedings against Austria (Art 258 TFEU), state liability (Köbler) and, under Austrian law, a violation of the right to the lawful judge (Art 83(2) B-VG). The party itself has no right to force a referral.
• The obligation: the OGH decides at last instance, so it must refer (Art 267(3)). No CILFIT exception applies. The question is new, and divergent case law in other Member States indicates reasonable doubt; a court that does not refer must also give reasons (Consorzio Italian Management, C-561/19).
• EU law: (1) Art 258. Acts of national courts are attributable to the Member State, so the Commission can bring infringement proceedings. In Commission v France (C-416/17) the Court for the first time found a breach of Art 267(3) by a supreme court. (2) Köbler (C-224/01): state liability if the breach is manifest, and failure to refer is an explicit factor in that assessment.
• Austrian law: parties have no subjective right to a referral (OGH 1 Ob 354/97h). But the CJEU counts as a "lawful judge" under Art 83(2) B-VG, and an unjustified failure to refer violates that constitutional right. Against administrative courts the remedy is a complaint to the VfGH (Art 144 B-VG). Against the OGH itself there is no further domestic remedy.
• ECHR: an arbitrary or unreasoned refusal to refer can breach Art 6(1) ECHR (e.g. Dhahbi v Italy, 2014).
Codex: Arts 258, 267(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU, Art 47 Charter; Art 83(2) B-VG; Art 6(1) ECHR · Cases: CILFIT (283/81), Consorzio Italian Management (C-561/19), Köbler (C-224/01), Commission v France (C-416/17).

cards.q: Which of the following bodies may make a preliminary reference under Article 267 TFEU? (a) A federal public procurement review board. It is established by statute, its members serve fixed terms and cannot be removed, and it decides procurement disputes on the basis of law after hearing both sides, with binding effect. (b) An arbitral tribunal set up under a contract between two shipbuilding companies. (c) The head of a national tax administration deciding on objections against tax assessments issued by his own staff. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only (a). Bodies (b) and (c) are not a "court or tribunal of a Member State" in the autonomous EU-law sense.
• Criteria (Vaassen-Göbbels 61/65; Dorsch Consult C-54/96): the body is established by law, is permanent, has compulsory jurisdiction, follows an inter partes (adversarial) procedure, applies rules of law, and is independent. Recent case law adds that its decision must be of a judicial nature. The national label does not matter.
• (a) All criteria are met, so it may refer (Dorsch Consult accepted a German federal procurement review board).
• (b) An arbitral tribunal has no compulsory jurisdiction, because the parties chose arbitration freely and the state is not involved. It cannot refer (Nordsee, 102/81). An ordinary court that reviews or enforces the award can.
• (c) An administrative authority deciding on acts of its own department is not independent and is not a third party (Corbiau, C-24/92).
Codex: Art 267(2)–(3) TFEU, Art 19(3)(b) TEU · Cases: Vaassen-Göbbels (61/65), Dorsch Consult (C-54/96), Nordsee (102/81), Corbiau (C-24/92).

cards.q: The Austrian Verwaltungsgerichtshof (VwGH), whose decisions cannot be appealed, must interpret a term in the VAT Directive. Must it refer in each of the following variants? (a) The CJEU has already answered an identical question in a case from Germany. (b) There is no CJEU case law and the VwGH thinks the answer is "obvious", but a Dutch supreme court has interpreted the term differently. (c) The question is irrelevant to the outcome of the case. (d) The question concerns the validity of the directive, which the VwGH considers invalid. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No (acte éclairé). (b) Yes, because the divergence rules out acte clair. (c) No (irrelevance). (d) Yes (Foto-Frost).
• Rule: under Art 267(3), a court against whose decisions there is no judicial remedy under national law must refer questions of interpretation that are raised and necessary for its decision.
• CILFIT (283/81) exceptions: the question is irrelevant; the question has already been decided in a materially identical case (acte éclairé; Da Costa, 28-30/62) or settled case law resolves the point; or the correct application of EU law is so obvious that there is no room for reasonable doubt (acte clair). For acte clair the court must be convinced the answer is equally obvious to the courts of other Member States and to the CJEU, bearing in mind the features of EU law: different language versions, its own terminology, and its context.
• Consorzio Italian Management (C-561/19, 2021): divergent lines of case law within or between Member States are a sign of reasonable doubt. A court that does not refer must state which exception applies.
• (a) Acte éclairé, so no duty, though the court may refer again. (b) Divergence means reasonable doubt, so it must refer. (c) No duty, because only necessary questions must be referred (Art 267(2)). (d) No national court may declare an EU act invalid (Foto-Frost, 314/85), so it must refer. The CILFIT exceptions do not apply to invalidity.
Codex: Art 267(1)–(3) TFEU · Cases: CILFIT (283/81), Da Costa (28-30/62), Consorzio Italian Management (C-561/19), Foto-Frost (314/85).

cards.q: An importer asks a German first-instance fiscal court to suspend a customs-duty demand issued on the basis of a Commission regulation that the importer considers invalid for breach of proportionality. The court shares the importer's doubts. (a) May the court declare the regulation invalid and annul the demand? (b) May it at least suspend enforcement until a ruling is given? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No. Only the CJEU may declare an EU act invalid, so the court must refer (Foto-Frost, 314/85). (b) Yes, but only under strict EU-law conditions (Zuckerfabrik Süderdithmarschen, C-143/88 and C-92/89; Atlanta, C-465/93).
• Art 267(1)(b): the CJEU rules on the validity of acts of the institutions. National courts may reject a plea of invalidity, but they may not declare an act invalid. Reasons: uniformity of EU law, the coherence of the system of remedies (annulment is reserved to the EU courts, Art 263), and legal certainty. This applies at every instance, even though Art 267(2) says "may".
• Interim relief: a national court may suspend a national measure based on an EU act, or grant positive interim measures, if (1) it has serious doubts about validity and refers the question itself (unless it is already pending); (2) there is urgency, meaning serious and irreparable damage to the applicant; (3) it takes due account of the Union's interest; and (4) it respects any decision of the EU courts on the act's legality.
• A ruling of invalidity has erga omnes effect: every other national court may treat the act as invalid (International Chemical Corporation, 66/80). It applies ex tunc unless the Court limits its temporal effect.
Codex: Arts 263, 267 TFEU, Art 19(1) TEU · Cases: Foto-Frost (314/85), Zuckerfabrik Süderdithmarschen (C-143/88 and C-92/89), Atlanta (C-465/93), International Chemical Corporation (66/80).

cards.q: In May 2015 a London borough fined Maxitaxi, a company operating a fleet of radio-dispatch taxis ("minicabs"), because one of its drivers used a bus lane in the city centre. In London both London Taxis ("black cabs") and minicabs carry paying passengers, but the boroughs allow only black cabs to use bus lanes. Maxitaxi argues that the bus-lane rule is unlawful state aid in favour of black cabs. The first-instance court hearing the case is unsure how to interpret certain provisions of EU state aid law. (a) Which procedure before the Court of Justice could help here, and where is it regulated? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: The preliminary reference procedure under Art 267 TFEU (together with Art 19(3)(b) TEU, Arts 23 and 23a of the Statute and Arts 93 ff. of the Rules of Procedure).
• The first-instance court is a "court or tribunal". It may refer questions on the interpretation of EU law, here Arts 107(1) and 108(3) TFEU, if they are necessary for its judgment (Art 267(2)). It stays its proceedings until the CJEU answers. The real case was Eventech (C-518/13, 2015).
Codex: Art 267 TFEU, Art 19(3)(b) TEU, Arts 107–108 TFEU · Case: Eventech (C-518/13).

cards.q: In May 2015 a London borough fined Maxitaxi, a company operating a fleet of radio-dispatch taxis ("minicabs"), because one of its drivers used a bus lane in the city centre. In London both London Taxis ("black cabs") and minicabs carry paying passengers, but the boroughs allow only black cabs to use bus lanes. Maxitaxi argues that the bus-lane rule is unlawful state aid in favour of black cabs. The first-instance court hearing the case is unsure how to interpret certain provisions of EU state aid law. (b) What would be the aim of such a procedure in this case? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: To obtain a binding interpretation of EU state aid law (Art 107(1) TFEU), so that the national court itself can decide whether the bus-lane rule is aid. The CJEU does not decide the case and does not rule on the national measure.
• Typical questions: does bus-lane access for black cabs involve state resources? Does it confer a selective advantage? Does it distort competition and affect trade between Member States?
• Purpose: uniform interpretation of EU law across the Member States, through cooperation between courts. The ruling binds the referring court and every court in the same proceedings, and in practice other courts must follow it too (erga omnes effect).
Codex: Arts 107(1), 108(3), 267 TFEU · Cases: Eventech (C-518/13), CILFIT (283/81).

cards.q: In May 2015 a London borough fined Maxitaxi, a company operating a fleet of radio-dispatch taxis ("minicabs"), because one of its drivers used a bus lane in the city centre. In London both London Taxis ("black cabs") and minicabs carry paying passengers, but the boroughs allow only black cabs to use bus lanes. Maxitaxi argues that the bus-lane rule is unlawful state aid in favour of black cabs. The first-instance court hearing the case is unsure how to interpret certain provisions of EU state aid law. (c) Does Maxitaxi have the right to demand that the national court start such a procedure? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. The parties have no right to a reference. The decision belongs to the national court alone ("may", Art 267(2)), and this first-instance court is not obliged to refer.
• The parties can suggest questions, but the procedure is a dialogue between courts, not a remedy for the parties (CILFIT). Only courts of last instance are obliged to refer (Art 267(3)). An unjustified refusal there can lead to Köbler liability, to proceedings under Art 258 and, in Austria, to a violation of Art 83(2) B-VG. Maxitaxi cannot apply to the CJEU directly.
Codex: Art 267(2)–(3) TFEU · Cases: CILFIT (283/81), Köbler (C-224/01).

cards.q: In May 2015 a London borough fined Maxitaxi, a company operating a fleet of radio-dispatch taxis ("minicabs"), because one of its drivers used a bus lane in the city centre. In London both London Taxis ("black cabs") and minicabs carry paying passengers, but the boroughs allow only black cabs to use bus lanes. Maxitaxi argues that the bus-lane rule is unlawful state aid in favour of black cabs. The first-instance court hearing the case is unsure how to interpret certain provisions of EU state aid law. (d) The national court would also like to know whether it is compatible with EU law that black cabs may be hailed in the street while minicabs must be pre-booked. How would the Court of Justice deal with such a question? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: The CJEU does not rule on whether national law is compatible with EU law. It would reformulate the question as one about interpreting EU law and give the national court the criteria. Here the hailing/pre-booking difference matters under Art 107(1): it shows that black cabs and minicabs are not in a comparable legal and factual situation, which speaks against selectivity (Eventech, C-518/13).
• Correction of a common answer: Art 56 TFEU would not help. Transport services fall under the transport title (Art 58(1) TFEU), and a purely internal London situation has no cross-border element. A question that is not needed for the dispute, or is hypothetical, is inadmissible (Art 267(2): "necessary").
Codex: Arts 58(1), 107(1), 267 TFEU · Case: Eventech (C-518/13).

cards.q: In 2015 the CJEU ruled in a preliminary reference that a Scottish minimum price per unit of alcohol restricts the free movement of goods, and that the national court must determine whether less restrictive measures, such as higher excise duties, could protect health equally well. The first-instance court finds that less restrictive means exist and does not apply the minimum-price law. On appeal, the higher court holds that it is not bound by the CJEU's judgment, overturns the first-instance judgment and applies the minimum-price law without further reflection. What do you say about this? What can the European Commission do if it learns of the situation? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The higher court is breaching EU law. A preliminary ruling binds every national court deciding the same case, including appeal courts, and primacy requires the incompatible law to be disapplied. The Commission can bring infringement proceedings against the Member State (Art 258 TFEU).
• Binding effect: the interpretation given under Art 267 binds the referring court and every court ruling in later stages of the same case (inter partes). In practice it also binds other courts (erga omnes): they may refer again but may not disregard it. A higher court with doubts must make a new reference, and as a court of last instance it is obliged to (Art 267(3)).
• Applying the law "without further reflection" also ignores primacy (Costa; Simmenthal) and the duty of sincere cooperation (Art 4(3) TEU). It is for the Member State to prove that the measure is proportionate.
• Commission: Art 258 procedure (letter of formal notice, reasoned opinion, action before the Court of Justice). Judicial acts are attributable to the state (Commission v France, C-416/17; Commission v Italy, C-129/00). If that judgment is then ignored, Art 260(2) follows. Traders harmed can claim Köbler damages.
Codex: Arts 34, 36, 258, 260(2), 267 TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU · Cases: Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14), Simmenthal (106/77), Köbler (C-224/01), Commission v France (C-416/17).

cards.q: A directive adopted under Article 114 TFEU harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances, including a maximum concentration for the chemical "PCP". Years later a Spanish study concludes that the permitted concentration may be too high, and Spain adopts new, stricter national rules. The Commission examines this national "solo action", considers it unjustified and wants to bring infringement proceedings. (b) Does the Commission have to follow a pre-litigation procedure? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under the general rule of Art 258 TFEU, yes: a letter of formal notice and then a reasoned opinion. But where a Member State makes improper use of the derogations in Art 114, Art 114(9) TFEU allows the Commission (or any Member State) to take the matter directly to the Court, by way of derogation from Arts 258 and 259.
• Art 258: the pre-litigation stage gives the state a chance to comment and fixes the subject-matter of the later action. Art 114(9) is an accelerated route, e.g. where Spain applies stricter rules without the Commission's approval or despite a rejection decision under Art 114(6).
Codex: Art 114(4)–(9) TFEU, Art 258 TFEU.

cards.q: A directive adopted under Article 114 TFEU harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances, including a maximum concentration for the chemical "PCP". Years later a Spanish study concludes that the permitted concentration may be too high, and Spain adopts new, stricter national rules. The Commission examines this national "solo action", considers it unjustified and wants to bring infringement proceedings. (c) Does the Commission have to prove its own legal interest in the case? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. As guardian of the Treaties (Art 17(1) TEU), the Commission acts in the general interest. The infringement procedure is objective, so the Commission need not show any specific interest or damage (Commission v Germany, C-431/92). It also has discretion whether and when to act.
• It must prove only the alleged failure, and the burden of proof is on it. Individuals cannot compel it to act (Star Fruit, 247/87).
Codex: Art 17(1) TEU, Art 258 TFEU · Cases: Commission v Germany (C-431/92), Star Fruit (247/87).

cards.q: A directive adopted under Article 114 TFEU harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances, including a maximum concentration for the chemical "PCP". Years later a Spanish study concludes that the permitted concentration may be too high, and Spain adopts new, stricter national rules. The Commission examines this national "solo action", considers it unjustified and wants to bring infringement proceedings. (d) What legal effect does a judgment establishing an infringement have? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: It is declaratory. It finds that the Member State has failed to fulfil its obligations, and under Art 260(1) the state must take the necessary measures to comply. The Court cannot annul national law or order specific measures.
• All national authorities, courts included, must draw the consequences, e.g. by disapplying the rule. If Spain does not comply, a second procedure under Art 260(2) follows, in which the COURT, not the Commission, may impose a lump sum and/or penalty payment on the Commission's proposal.
Codex: Art 260(1)–(2) TFEU.

cards.q: A directive adopted under Article 114 TFEU harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances, including a maximum concentration for the chemical "PCP". Years later a Spanish study concludes that the permitted concentration may be too high, and Spain adopts new, stricter national rules. The Commission examines this national "solo action", considers it unjustified and wants to bring infringement proceedings. (e) Is an appeal against the Court's judgment possible? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. The Court of Justice decides infringement actions at first and last instance (Art 258 with Art 256(1) TFEU and Art 51 Statute), so its judgment is final.
• Appeals exist only against decisions of the General Court (Art 256(1), second subparagraph). The only further steps are extraordinary: interpretation of the judgment (Art 43 Statute) or revision if a decisive new fact is discovered (Art 44 Statute).
Codex: Arts 256(1), 258 TFEU; Arts 43, 44, 51 Statute.

cards.q: Directive 2010/76/EU on the remuneration policies of banks was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure. After the transposition deadline, Italy has still not fully implemented it, and the Commission brings an action before the Court of Justice. Can financial penalties be imposed immediately in these proceedings? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Under Art 260(3) TFEU, where the Commission brings an Art 258 action because a Member State failed to notify measures transposing a directive adopted under a legislative procedure, the Commission may propose, and the Court may impose, a lump sum and/or penalty payment already in the first judgment.
• Directive 2010/76 is a legislative act (Art 289 TFEU). "Not fully implemented" means notification is incomplete, which Art 260(3) covers (Commission v Belgium, C-543/17). The Court may not exceed the amount the Commission specifies. The pre-litigation procedure is still required.
Codex: Arts 258, 260(3), 289(3) TFEU · Case: Commission v Belgium (C-543/17).

cards.q: The Commission wants financial penalties imposed already in the first infringement judgment.
