Is Article 260(3) TFEU available where: (a) State X has notified no transposition measures at all for a directive adopted by Parliament and the Council; (b) State Y has notified measures covering only half of the directive's provisions; (c) State Z has notified complete measures, but the Commission considers one provision incorrectly transposed; (d) the directive was adopted by the Commission as a delegated act? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes. (b) Yes. (c) No. (d) No.
• Art 260(3) applies where a Member State "has failed to fulfil its obligation to notify measures transposing a directive adopted under a legislative procedure", ordinary or special (Art 289). It is an exception to the two-stage system of Art 260(1)–(2), designed to push states to transpose on time.
• (a) Total failure to notify is the classic case.
• (b) Partial notification: under Commission v Belgium (C-543/17, 2019), the duty to notify covers measures transposing every provision of the directive, so incomplete notification falls within Art 260(3).
• (c) Incorrect transposition is not covered. Where measures have been notified but their content is defective, the Commission would have to assess substantive conformity, which is beyond Art 260(3). The ordinary route is Art 258 and then Art 260(2).
• (d) A delegated directive (Art 290) is a non-legislative act, so Art 260(3) does not apply.
• In every case the amount proposed by the Commission is the ceiling, and the payment obligation takes effect on the date set by the Court.
Codex: Arts 258, 260(1)–(3), 289–290 TFEU · Case: Commission v Belgium (C-543/17).

cards.q: In 2022 the Court of Justice found that State Tarsis had infringed EU waste law by operating illegal landfills. Three years later the landfills are still in operation. What can the Commission do, which sanctions are possible, and how are they set? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Commission can open a second procedure under Art 260(2) TFEU. After giving Tarsis the opportunity to submit observations, it can ask the Court to impose a lump sum and/or a periodic penalty payment. The Court decides in its discretion.
• Procedure: since Lisbon only a letter of formal notice is needed before referring the case back to the Court, with no reasoned opinion. The Commission states the amount it considers appropriate. Under Art 260(2), unlike Art 260(3), the Court is not bound by that proposal.
• Sanctions: a lump sum punishes the past period of non-compliance, and a penalty payment (per day or per half-year) runs until the state complies. Both can be imposed together (Commission v France, C-304/02).
• Criteria: the seriousness and duration of the infringement, the need for deterrence, and the Member State's ability to pay.
• The money goes to the EU budget. If it is not paid, the Commission can offset it against payments due to the state.
Codex: Arts 258, 260(1)–(2) TFEU · Case: Commission v France (C-304/02).

cards.q: Austria considers that Germany's new motorway toll discriminates against drivers from other Member States, because German car owners are in effect fully compensated through a reduction in vehicle tax. The Commission refuses to act. Can Austria itself take Germany to the Court of Justice, and what procedure must it follow? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Under Art 259 TFEU a Member State may bring infringement proceedings against another Member State. It must first bring the matter before the Commission. Once the Commission has delivered a reasoned opinion, or if it has not done so within three months, Austria can go to the Court. This happened in Austria v Germany (C-591/17, 2019), which Austria won.
• Art 259(3)–(4): the Commission gives both states the chance to present their case and observations, orally and in writing, and then delivers a reasoned opinion. A refusal or negative opinion does not bar the action.
• The action goes to the Court of Justice, and the judgment is declaratory (Art 260).
• Substance of C-591/17: the combination of toll and tax relief was indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality (Art 18 TFEU) and infringed the free movement of goods and services (Arts 34, 56) and the transport standstill clause (Art 92).
Codex: Arts 18, 259, 260 TFEU · Case: Austria v Germany (C-591/17).

cards.q: Comment on the following statements, say whether each is true or false, and give reasons. (a) "A company harmed by a Member State's breach of EU law can compel the Commission to start infringement proceedings, if necessary by an action for failure to act." (b) "Individuals can bring an action directly before the Court of Justice against a Member State that violates EU law." (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both are false.
• (a) False. The Commission has discretion under Art 258 ("may") whether and when to start proceedings. Its refusal is not a reviewable act, and an action for failure to act (Art 265) is inadmissible (Lütticke, 48/65; Star Fruit, 247/87). A complaint to the Commission is possible, informal and free, but it creates no right to proceedings. The European Ombudsman can review maladministration in how the complaint was handled (Art 228 TFEU).
• (b) False. There is no direct action by individuals against Member States before the CJEU. Individuals rely on EU law before national courts (direct effect, primacy, Francovich), and those courts may or must refer (Art 267). Art 263(4) lies only against EU acts.
Codex: Arts 228, 258, 263(4), 265, 267 TFEU · Cases: Lütticke (48/65), Star Fruit (247/87).

cards.q: Which court decides at first instance on: (a) an action for annulment by a company against a Commission competition decision; (b) an action for annulment by a Member State against a directive of Parliament and the Council; (c) an infringement action by the Commission; (d) a preliminary reference from an Austrian court on the interpretation of the VAT Directive? What appeal is possible? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) The General Court. (b) The Court of Justice. (c) The Court of Justice. (d) Since 1 October 2024, in principle the General Court, because VAT is one of the transferred areas. Otherwise the Court of Justice.
• Art 256(1) TFEU with Art 51 Statute: the General Court hears direct actions under Arts 263, 265, 268, 270 and 272 at first instance, except those reserved to the Court of Justice. These include, in particular, actions by Member States against acts of Parliament and/or the Council (with exceptions) and actions between institutions. Appeals on points of law go to the Court of Justice within two months (Art 56 Statute), plus ten days on account of distance.
• Art 256(3): the General Court may hear preliminary references in specific areas laid down in the Statute. Since 2024 these are VAT, excise duties, the Customs Code, tariff classification, passenger compensation (denied boarding, delay, cancellation) and emissions trading (Art 50b Statute). All references are lodged with the Court of Justice, which forwards those in these areas.
• Judgments of the Court of Justice in infringement cases cannot be appealed.
Codex: Art 256(1), (3) TFEU; Art 19(1) TEU; Arts 50b, 51, 56 Statute.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: As part of the EU's response to the financial crisis, Directive 2010/76/EU was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure. It requires banks and investment firms to follow sound remuneration policies and so to eliminate excessive pay incentives. One day after its publication in the Official Journal, an Austrian bank learns of the directive and considers it incompatible with EU primary law. (a) How, and under what conditions, could the bank challenge this act within the EU system of legal protection? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only by an action for annulment under Art 263(4) TFEU before the General Court, within two months. As a non-privileged applicant challenging a legislative directive not addressed to it, the bank must show direct AND individual concern, which it almost certainly cannot. The realistic route is indirect review through the national courts and Art 267.
• Reviewable act: a legislative act of Parliament and the Council (Art 263(1)). The General Court has jurisdiction (Art 256(1)).
• Standing: the bank is non-privileged (Art 263(4)) and not an addressee, because directives are addressed to Member States (Art 288(3)). The "regulatory act" limb is closed: the directive is a legislative act (Inuit, C-583/11 P) and needs national transposition. So direct and individual concern is required.
• Direct concern is lacking, because the directive affects the bank only through national transposing measures that involve discretion. Individual concern is lacking, because the bank belongs to an open class of all credit institutions (Plaumann, 25/62).
• Time limit: two months from publication (Art 263(6)), plus 14 days and 10 days on account of distance (Arts 59–60 Rules of Procedure of the General Court). When the bank learned of the directive is irrelevant. Grounds: Art 263(2).
Codex: Art 263(1), (2), (4), (6), Arts 256(1), 288(3), 289(3) TFEU · Cases: Plaumann (25/62), Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (C-583/11 P).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: As part of the EU's response to the financial crisis, Directive 2010/76/EU was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure. It requires banks and investment firms to follow sound remuneration policies and so to eliminate excessive pay incentives. One day after its publication in the Official Journal, an Austrian bank learns of the directive and considers it incompatible with EU primary law. (b) Assume the bank's action is admissible and well founded. What are the consequences of a successful action, and what binding effect does the judgment have? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The General Court declares the directive, or its severable contested provisions, void (Art 264(1) TFEU), with effect ex tunc and erga omnes. The institutions concerned must take the measures needed to comply (Art 266 TFEU).
• The act is void from the start and for everyone, not only between the parties. Member States no longer have to transpose it, and national transposing laws lose their EU basis.
• Art 264(2): the Court may state which effects of the annulled act are to be treated as definitive, e.g. to protect legal certainty or avoid a regulatory gap until a new act is adopted.
• Art 266: Parliament and the Council must comply with the operative part and the grounds that support it, e.g. by adopting a new, lawful act. The unlawfulness may also found a damages action (Arts 268, 340(2)).
• Appeal on points of law to the Court of Justice (Art 256(1), second subparagraph; Art 56 Statute).
Codex: Arts 256(1), 264, 266, 268, 340(2) TFEU; Art 56 Statute.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: As part of the EU's response to the financial crisis, Directive 2010/76/EU was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure. It requires banks and investment firms to follow sound remuneration policies and so to eliminate excessive pay incentives. One day after its publication in the Official Journal, an Austrian bank learns of the directive and considers it incompatible with EU primary law. (c) The General Court dismisses the bank's action as inadmissible for lack of standing. Austria transposes the directive by amending its Banking Act, and the Financial Market Authority (FMA) orders the bank to cut its bonuses. What options does the bank still have to challenge the directive's validity, and what role could the Republic of Austria have played? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The bank can challenge the FMA order in the Austrian courts and plead that the directive is invalid. If the court has doubts, it must refer the validity question to the CJEU (Foto-Frost). Austria, as a privileged applicant, could itself have brought an action for annulment within two months.
• Indirect review through a validity reference (Art 267(1)(b)). The Treaties form a "complete system of legal remedies" (Les Verts, 294/83; UPA, C-50/00 P): where individuals lack standing under Art 263(4), they must be able to challenge implementing measures nationally, and Member States must provide the remedies (Art 19(1)(2) TEU).
• No preclusion: under TWD (C-188/92), a party cannot plead invalidity nationally only if it would undoubtedly have had standing under Art 263 and let the time limit pass. That is not the case here.
• The national court may reject the plea. If it has doubts it must refer (Foto-Frost, 314/85), and the last-instance court (VwGH) is in any case obliged to refer (Art 267(3)). Interim relief is possible under the Zuckerfabrik conditions.
• A plea of illegality under Art 277 is not available: it can be raised only in proceedings before the EU courts, not in national proceedings.
• Austria is fully privileged (Art 263(2)). It could have sued within two months without showing any interest, and the bank could have lobbied the government to do so.
Codex: Art 263(2), (4), (6), Arts 267, 277 TFEU; Art 19(1) TEU · Cases: Les Verts (294/83), UPA (C-50/00 P), TWD Textilwerke Deggendorf (C-188/92), Foto-Frost (314/85), Zuckerfabrik (C-143/88).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Which claimants are fully privileged in actions for annulment, and which are semi-privileged? Under which conditions can non-privileged claimants bring an action? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Fully privileged are the Member States, Parliament, the Council and the Commission (Art 263(2) TFEU). Semi-privileged are the Court of Auditors, the ECB and the Committee of the Regions, but only to protect their prerogatives (Art 263(3)). Non-privileged natural and legal persons may sue if they are the addressee, if the act is of direct and individual concern to them, or if it is a regulatory act of direct concern to them that entails no implementing measures (Art 263(4)).
• Non-privileged applicants include regions and municipalities (which are not the Member State as such), companies and NGOs.
• Direct concern (needed in both of the last two alternatives): the act directly affects the applicant's legal situation and leaves no discretion to those who implement it, so implementation is purely automatic (Dreyfus, C-386/96 P). A merely factual or potential effect is not enough.
• Individual concern (Plaumann, 25/62): the act affects the applicant because of attributes peculiar to it, or circumstances that set it apart from all other persons, distinguishing it individually just as an addressee would be. Examples: a closed class, participation in the procedure leading to the act, specific rights (Codorniu, C-309/89: a trademark).
• Regulatory act: a non-legislative act of general application (Inuit, C-583/11 P) that entails no implementing measures for the applicant (Telefónica, C-274/12 P). Individual concern is then not required (Microban, T-262/10).
• Also required: the two-month time limit (Art 263(6)) and an interest in bringing proceedings.
Codex: Art 263(1)–(4), (6) TFEU · Cases: Plaumann (25/62), Codorniu (C-309/89), Dreyfus (C-386/96 P), Inuit (C-583/11 P), Telefónica (C-274/12 P), Microban (T-262/10).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Germany asks the Commission for authorisation to suspend customs duties on clementines imported from third countries. The Commission refuses by a decision addressed to Germany. Plaumann & Co., one of several German clementine importers, wants the decision annulled. (a) Is Plaumann individually concerned? (b) Would the answer change if the decision concerned only import licences already applied for, by a closed list of identifiable importers, before it was adopted? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No. Importing clementines is a commercial activity that anyone may take up at any time, so the action is inadmissible (Plaumann, 25/62). (b) Yes. If the decision affects a closed class of identifiable persons fixed when it is adopted, such as pending licence applicants, they are individually concerned (Toepfer, 106 and 107/63; International Fruit Company, 41-44/70).
• Art 263(4): Plaumann is not the addressee (Germany is), and the act is an individual decision, not a regulatory act. So direct and individual concern must be shown. The Court did not need to examine direct concern once individual concern failed.
• Plaumann formula: the act must affect the applicant because of attributes peculiar to it, or circumstances that differentiate it from all other persons, distinguishing it individually just as an addressee would be. Being one of a few current importers is not enough while the class remains open.
• (b) Closed class: the Commission knew, or could know, the applicants at the time, and the decision in effect settled their applications, so they are individualised like addressees.
• Criticism: in UPA (C-50/00 P) and Jégo-Quéré (C-263/02 P) the Court refused to relax Plaumann. The gap is filled by Art 19(1)(2) TEU (national remedies) and by the "regulatory act" limb introduced by Lisbon.
Codex: Art 263(4) TFEU, Art 19(1) TEU · Cases: Plaumann (25/62), Toepfer (106 and 107/63), International Fruit Company (41-44/70), Codorniu (C-309/89), UPA (C-50/00 P), Jégo-Quéré (C-263/02 P).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: By a non-legislative decision of general application adopted under comitology, the Commission removes the antibacterial substance triclosan from the list of additives permitted in plastics that come into contact with food. From a set date, such plastics containing triclosan may no longer be marketed, and no national or EU implementing measures are needed. Microban, a producer of triclosan-based additives, wants the decision annulled. It is not an addressee and is not distinguished from other producers. Is the action admissible? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. The decision is a regulatory act of direct concern to Microban that entails no implementing measures, so under the third limb of Art 263(4) TFEU individual concern is not required (Microban, T-262/10).
• Regulatory act (Inuit, C-583/11 P): an act of general application that is not a legislative act. A Commission implementing or delegated measure qualifies. A legislative act (Art 289(3)) would not.
• No implementing measures: the ban applies directly from the set date. This is assessed from the applicant's position (Telefónica, C-274/12 P). If national authorities had to adopt measures, even mechanical ones, this limb would be closed.
• Direct concern: the decision directly affects Microban's legal situation, since it may no longer market its additive for this use, and nobody implementing it has any discretion.
• Time limit: two months, plus 14 days after publication and 10 days on account of distance.
• Contrast: had the ban been in a legislative regulation of Parliament and the Council, Microban would need individual concern under Plaumann and would probably fail, as the Inuit applicants did against the seal-products regulation.
Codex: Art 263(4), (6), Arts 289(3), 290–291 TFEU · Cases: Microban (T-262/10), Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (C-583/11 P), Telefónica (C-274/12 P).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Which of the following can be challenged under Article 263 TFEU? (a) A Commission letter informing a company that it has opened a formal competition investigation against it. (b) A Commission decision fining a cartel. (c) A Council "resolution", not one of the acts listed in Art 288, setting the Member States' negotiating position for an international transport agreement and intended to bind them. (d) A Commission recommendation. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (b) and (c) can be challenged. (a) and (d) cannot.
• Test: any measure of an EU institution, body, office or agency, whatever its form or name, that is intended to produce binding legal effects capable of affecting the applicant's interests by clearly changing its legal position (ERTA, 22/70; IBM, 60/81). Art 263(1) excludes recommendations and opinions.
• (a) This is a preparatory step, like opening proceedings or a statement of objections. It fixes no final position, so only the final decision can be challenged (IBM).
• (b) A final decision with binding effects for its addressee (Art 288(4)): yes.
• (c) ERTA: the Council's act was meant to lay down a binding course of action for the institutions and the Member States, so it is reviewable whatever its form.
• (d) Recommendations are not binding (Art 288(5)) and are excluded by Art 263(1), unless the act is in substance binding.
Codex: Art 263(1), Art 288 TFEU · Cases: ERTA (22/70), IBM (60/81).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: A Council regulation fixing sugar production quotas was adopted under a Treaty provision that requires the European Parliament to be consulted. Under which ground of annulment does each of the following pleas fall? (a) The Council adopted the regulation before Parliament gave its opinion, although the Council had asked for it. (b) The regulation contains no statement of reasons. (c) The Council used its agricultural powers mainly to protect domestic producers against competitors from one particular Member State, a purpose the legal basis does not cover. (d) The regulation breaches the principle of equal treatment. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) and (b) are infringements of an essential procedural requirement. (c) is misuse of powers. (d) is infringement of the Treaties or of any rule of law relating to their application. The fourth ground, lack of competence, is not raised here.
• Art 263(2) lists four grounds. Lack of competence: the Union or the institution lacks the power, e.g. wrong legal basis or acting ultra vires (Tobacco Advertising, C-376/98). Infringement of an essential procedural requirement. Infringement of the Treaties or any rule of law relating to their application, which includes the Charter, general principles such as proportionality and equal treatment, and international agreements binding the Union. Misuse of powers: a power used for a purpose other than the one for which it was conferred.
• (a) Consulting Parliament reflects the fundamental democratic principle. Adopting the act before Parliament's opinion leads to annulment (Roquette Frères, 138/79, isoglucose), unless Parliament itself obstructs the procedure.
• (b) The duty to state reasons (Art 296(2) TFEU) is an essential procedural requirement.
• (c) Misuse of powers must be shown by objective, relevant and consistent evidence that the act was adopted exclusively or mainly for an improper purpose.
• (d) Equal treatment is a general principle and is laid down in Art 20 Charter.
• If a plea succeeds, the act is declared void (Art 264).
Codex: Art 263(2), Art 264, Art 296(2) TFEU; Art 20 Charter · Cases: Roquette Frères (138/79), Tobacco Advertising (C-376/98).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: In January, Tecno, a software company, lodged a complaint with the Commission that a dominant competitor is abusing its position (Article 102 TFEU). Nothing happened. In June Tecno sends a formal letter calling on the Commission to decide on its complaint. By the end of August the Commission has still not replied. (a) Which action is available, until when, and before which court? (b) What if the Commission had replied in July with a letter rejecting the complaint? (c) What can the Court order? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) An action for failure to act under Art 265 TFEU before the General Court, which must be brought within a further two months after the two-month period following the call to act has expired. (b) A rejection is a "definition of position" that ends the failure, so Tecno would have to challenge the rejection by an action for annulment (Art 263). (c) Only a declaration that the failure to act was unlawful.
• Admissibility: (1) a duty to act. The Commission must examine complaints and, if it does not pursue them, reject them by decision (Reg 773/2004, Art 7). (2) A prior call to act (Art 265(2)): the June letter. (3) No definition of position within two months: by the end of August. (4) The action is brought within a further two months: by the end of October, plus 10 days on account of distance. (5) Standing under Art 265(3): a natural or legal person may complain that an institution failed to address to it an act other than a recommendation or opinion. A complainant is entitled to a decision on its complaint.
• (b) A definition of position, even a negative one, ends the failure, so Art 265 becomes inadmissible. The rejection decision is reviewable under Art 263(4), with Tecno as its addressee.
• (c) The judgment is declaratory. Under Art 266 the Commission must take the necessary measures, i.e. decide, but it cannot be forced to adopt a decision with particular content. Damages must be claimed separately (Arts 268, 340(2)).
• Distinguish: Art 265 cannot be used to force the Commission to start infringement proceedings against a Member State (Lütticke, 48/65; Star Fruit, 247/87).
Codex: Art 256(1), Art 263(4), Art 265(1)–(3), Art 266 TFEU; Reg 1/2003, Art 7; Reg 773/2004, Art 7 · Cases: Lütticke (48/65), Star Fruit (247/87).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: In 2023 the Commission adopted a regulation laying down general rules on eligible costs under an EU research-funding programme. In 2025, by a decision addressed to Holtz GmbH, it orders Holtz to repay part of its grant, calculated under those rules. Holtz brings an action for annulment against the 2025 decision within two months and argues that the 2023 regulation itself breaches the programme's basic regulation. The Commission objects that the 2023 regulation can no longer be challenged. (a) Can Holtz raise the argument? (b) What happens if it succeeds? (c) Could Holtz raise the same argument before a national court? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes, by a plea of illegality under Art 277 TFEU, even though the Art 263(6) time limit for the regulation has expired. (b) The 2023 regulation is declared inapplicable in this case, and the 2025 decision based on it is annulled. The regulation itself is not annulled. (c) No. Art 277 applies only before the EU courts. Before a national court the equivalent is a validity reference (Art 267; Foto-Frost).
• Conditions: proceedings must be pending before the EU courts (here an action for annulment). The contested act must be an act of general application. It must be the legal basis of, or directly connected with, the individual act under challenge. The grounds are those in Art 263(2).
• Nature: an incidental plea, not an independent action. It protects parties who could not challenge a general act directly, usually for lack of standing, against its application to them (Simmenthal v Commission, 92/78).
• Limit: it does not cover acts the applicant could have challenged directly as their addressee, e.g. an individual decision addressed to it, because the time limit would otherwise be circumvented.
• Effect: inapplicability between the parties only. The institution must draw the consequences (Art 266).
Codex: Art 263(2), (6), Arts 266, 267, 277 TFEU · Cases: Simmenthal v Commission (92/78), Foto-Frost (314/85), TWD (C-188/92).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: The Commission adopts a regulation prohibiting the marketing of a cosmetic ingredient on health grounds, and Bergo, a producer, loses sales. It turns out that the ban was based on a scientific assessment made without consulting the scientific committee, as the basic regulation requires. Bergo claims compensation. (a) Which action, before which court, and within what time limit? (b) Under which conditions will it succeed? (c) Must Bergo first obtain annulment of the regulation? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) An action for damages under Arts 268 and 340(2) TFEU before the General Court, within five years. (b) The Bergaderm conditions: a sufficiently serious breach of a rule of law intended to confer rights on individuals, actual damage, and a direct causal link. (c) No. The damages action is autonomous.
• Art 340(2): in accordance with the general principles common to the laws of the Member States, the Union must make good any damage caused by its institutions or servants in performing their duties. The limitation period is five years from the event giving rise to liability (Art 46 Statute).
• Conditions: Bergaderm (C-352/98 P, 2000) aligned Union liability with Member State liability (Brasserie). The decisive test for seriousness is a manifest and grave disregard of the limits of discretion. Where discretion is reduced or absent, a mere infringement may be enough. The older Schöppenstedt formula (5/71) for legislative acts involving economic policy choices required a "sufficiently flagrant violation of a superior rule of law for the protection of the individual".
• Application: it is arguable whether a procedural rule requiring consultation of a scientific committee protects individuals. Where a complex scientific assessment involves wide discretion, a sufficiently serious breach is hard to prove. The claim in Bergaderm itself failed.
• (c) The action is autonomous (Lütticke, 4/69; Schöppenstedt), so no prior annulment is needed, but the unlawfulness must be proved within the damages action.
Codex: Arts 256(1), 268, 340(2) TFEU; Art 46 Statute · Cases: Bergaderm (C-352/98 P), Zuckerfabrik Schöppenstedt (5/71), Lütticke (4/69), Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Maria's company has brought an action for annulment against a Commission decision that orders it to stop selling a product within 30 days. (a) Does the action suspend the decision? (b) How can the company obtain interim protection, and under which conditions? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No. Actions before the EU courts have no suspensory effect (Art 278, first sentence, TFEU). (b) The company can apply to the President of the General Court for suspension of the decision (Art 278, second sentence) or for other interim measures (Art 279). It must show a prima facie case (fumus boni iuris), urgency (serious and irreparable damage) and a balance of interests in its favour.
• The applicant must be a party to pending main proceedings. The measures are provisional and do not prejudge the main case. They are ordered by the President (Art 39 Statute).
• Urgency: purely financial damage is normally not irreparable, unless it threatens the company's existence or would irreversibly change its market position.
Codex: Arts 278, 279 TFEU; Art 39 Statute.

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: (a) Did the EEC Treaty in its original version contain a written catalogue of fundamental and human rights? (1 point) (b) On what basis did the Court of Justice develop its case law on fundamental rights? Name well-known judgments. (2 points) (c) How has the Treaty of Lisbon changed the legal situation? (1 point) (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No. (b) The Court recognised fundamental rights as unwritten general principles of Community law, inspired by the constitutional traditions common to the Member States and by international human rights treaties, especially the ECHR (Stauder, Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, Nold). (c) Lisbon made the Charter legally binding with the same value as the Treaties (Art 6(1) TEU), provided for accession to the ECHR (Art 6(2)) and kept the general principles (Art 6(3)).
• (a) The EEC was an economic community. At first the Court refused to review Community acts against national fundamental rights (Stork, 1/58; Ruhrkohlen-Verkaufsgesellschaften, 36-38/59 and 40/59).
• (b) Direct effect and primacy created a gap in protection, and national constitutional courts pushed back (Solange I, 1974). Stauder (29/69): fundamental rights are "enshrined in the general principles of Community law and protected by the Court". Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70): the validity of Community acts cannot be judged by national constitutional law, but respect for fundamental rights is an integral part of the general principles, inspired by common constitutional traditions. Nold (4/73): international treaties on which the Member States collaborated or which they signed are also a source. Rutili (36/75): the ECHR is mentioned expressly. The German court's answer was Solange II (1986). Maastricht codified the approach (Art F(2) TEU).
• (c) The Charter was proclaimed at Nice in 2000 and became binding on 1 December 2009. Art 6(1) TEU makes it primary law; it does not extend EU competences and is interpreted with the Explanations. Art 6(2): obligation to accede to the ECHR (not yet achieved; Opinion 2/13). Art 6(3): general principles remain as a second pillar.
Codex: Art 6(1)–(3) TEU; Arts 51–53 Charter · Cases: Stauder (29/69), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70), Nold (4/73), Rutili (36/75); BVerfG Solange I (1974) and Solange II (1986).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: The Swedish tax authority orders Mr Hans, a fisherman, to pay tax surcharges (administrative penalties) for false VAT and income-tax returns. He is later prosecuted for tax fraud on the same facts, and he invokes the prohibition of double jeopardy (ne bis in idem) in Article 50 of the Charter. Sweden argues that the Charter does not apply, because the penalties rest on national laws that were not adopted to transpose EU law. (a) Does the Charter apply? (b) What follows for the national court? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes, at least for VAT. The penalties "implement Union law" within Art 51(1) Charter, because they serve to collect VAT under the VAT Directive and to protect the Union's financial interests under Art 325 TFEU (Åkerberg Fransson, C-617/10). (b) The national court must apply Art 50 Charter and, where necessary, disapply conflicting national law.
• Art 51(1): the Charter binds Member States "only when they are implementing Union law". Åkerberg Fransson reads this as any situation within the scope of EU law: "applicability of EU law entails applicability of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Charter". The reverse also holds: outside that scope the Charter does not apply (Art 51(2); Art 6(1) TEU).
• It does not matter that the national laws were not adopted to transpose EU law. The VAT Directive requires Member States to ensure VAT is collected, and Art 325 TFEU requires effective penalties against fraud affecting the EU's finances (VAT is an own resource).
• Ne bis in idem applies only if the tax surcharge is criminal in nature, assessed under the Engel criteria (classification in national law, nature of the offence, severity of the penalty). That is for the national court. A duplication of proceedings may be justified under Art 52(1) (Menci, C-524/15).
• National standards of protection may also apply, provided the Charter's level of protection and the primacy, unity and effectiveness of EU law are not compromised (Melloni, C-399/11).
• The income-tax part is outside the scope of EU law, so only national constitutional rights and the ECHR (Protocol 7, Art 4) apply there.
Codex: Art 6(1) TEU; Arts 50, 51, 52(1), 52(3), 53 Charter; Art 325 TFEU · Cases: Åkerberg Fransson (C-617/10), Melloni (C-399/11), Menci (C-524/15).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: An EU directive obliges telecom providers to retain all traffic and location data of all users for two years in order to fight serious crime, with no differentiation, no exceptions and no requirement of prior review by a court or independent body before the authorities gain access. A digital-rights group challenges the national implementing law, and the national court refers the question of the directive's validity to the CJEU. How will the Court assess it under the Charter? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The directive interferes with Arts 7 and 8 Charter. Under Art 52(1) Charter the interference pursues an objective of general interest and does not affect the essence of the rights, but it is not limited to what is strictly necessary. It is therefore disproportionate, and the directive is invalid (Digital Rights Ireland, C-293/12 and C-594/12).
• Art 52(1): a limitation must (1) be provided for by law, (2) respect the essence of the rights, and (3) be proportionate, i.e. necessary and genuinely meeting objectives of general interest recognised by the Union or the need to protect the rights and freedoms of others.
• Art 52(3): where Charter rights correspond to ECHR rights (Art 7 Charter and Art 8 ECHR), they have the same meaning and scope. The ECHR is a minimum, and EU law may give more protection.
• Application: fighting serious crime is a legitimate objective, and the essence is untouched because the content of communications is not retained. But general and indiscriminate retention of everyone's data, without criteria limiting access or duration and without independent prior review, goes beyond what is strictly necessary.
• Procedure: only the CJEU can declare the directive invalid (Foto-Frost). In 2014 it declared Directive 2006/24 invalid ab initio, on references from the Irish High Court and the Austrian Verfassungsgerichtshof.
Codex: Arts 7, 8, 52(1), 52(3) Charter; Art 6(1) TEU; Art 267 TFEU · Cases: Digital Rights Ireland (C-293/12 and C-594/12), Foto-Frost (314/85).

cards.topic: Annulment, Failure to Act and Fundamental Rights
cards.q: Is the EU bound by the European Convention on Human Rights? Why has the EU not (yet) acceded to it, although Article 6(2) TEU says that it "shall accede"? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not formally. The EU is not a party to the ECHR (only the Member States are), so the Convention binds it only indirectly, through the general principles (Art 6(3) TEU) and Art 52(3) Charter. Accession has so far failed because the Court of Justice found the draft accession agreement incompatible with the Treaties (Opinion 2/13, 2014). Earlier, Opinion 2/94 had found that the Community lacked the competence to accede.
• Opinion 2/94 (1996): no competence without Treaty amendment. Lisbon then added Art 6(2) TEU and Protocol No 8, and ECHR Protocol 14 opened the Convention to the EU (Art 59(2) ECHR).
• Opinion 2/13 objections: the agreement threatened the autonomy and specific characteristics of EU law. Art 53 ECHR and Art 53 Charter were not coordinated (Melloni). Mutual trust between Member States was undermined. ECHR Protocol 16 could be used to bypass Art 267. Art 344 TFEU was infringed because inter-state cases between Member States were not excluded. The co-respondent and prior-involvement mechanisms would let Strasbourg rule on EU law and on the division of competences. And the ECtHR would review CFSP acts that the CJEU itself largely cannot.
• Negotiations resumed, and a revised draft was agreed at negotiators' level in 2023. A new Court opinion, a unanimous Council decision and ratification by all Member States are still needed (Art 218(6), (8), (11) TFEU).
• Meanwhile the Member States remain answerable in Strasbourg for how they implement EU law, subject to the Bosphorus presumption of equivalent protection (ECtHR, 2005).
Codex: Art 6(2)–(3) TEU; Art 218(6), (8), (11) TFEU; Arts 52(3), 53 Charter; Protocol No 8 · Cases: Opinion 2/94, Opinion 2/13; ECtHR Bosphorus (2005).

cards.q: The Alcohol (Minimum Pricing) (Scotland) Act introduced a minimum retail price per unit of alcohol for all alcoholic drinks sold in Scotland. In a 2015 preliminary ruling the CJEU held that such rules could restrict the internal market, and that the national court must determine whether other, less restrictive measures could protect human health and life just as effectively while restricting trade within the Union less. (a) Which fundamental freedom is affected, and where is it regulated? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: The free movement of goods: Art 28 TFEU (the basic principle) and in particular Art 34 TFEU, which prohibits quantitative restrictions on imports and all measures having equivalent effect. Justification is governed by Art 36 TFEU.
• Art 30 (customs duties) and Art 110 (internal taxation) do not apply, because a minimum price is neither a duty nor a tax. The real case is Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14).
Codex: Arts 28, 34, 36 TFEU · Case: Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14).

cards.q: The Alcohol (Minimum Pricing) (Scotland) Act introduced a minimum retail price per unit of alcohol for all alcoholic drinks sold in Scotland. In a 2015 preliminary ruling the CJEU held that such rules could restrict the internal market, and that the national court must determine whether other, less restrictive measures could protect human health and life just as effectively while restricting trade within the Union less. (b) Under what conditions does the scope of this fundamental freedom apply? Does it apply here? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes, it applies. Alcoholic drinks are goods, many of them are imported from other Member States, the measure is a state measure attributable to the UK (then a Member State), and no exhaustive harmonisation displaces the Treaty test.
• Material scope: goods are products that have a monetary value and can be the subject of commercial transactions (Commission v Italy, 7/68). This covers goods originating in the Member States and third-country goods in free circulation (Art 28(2)).
• Cross-border element: trade between Member States must be at least potentially affected. Wine, spirits and beer from other Member States are sold at retail in Scotland, so this is not a purely internal situation.
• Addressee: Art 34 binds the Member States, meaning all public authorities, including devolved or regional legislators such as the Scottish Parliament.
• Secondary law first: if a field is exhaustively harmonised, the national measure is judged only against the harmonising act. The CMO Regulation 1308/2013 (wine) does not exhaustively regulate retail prices, so Art 34 applies. The Court examined both.
• Correction of a common answer: what matters is the goods and cross-border trade in them, not the nationality of the trader.
Codex: Arts 28(2), 34, 36 TFEU; Reg 1308/2013 · Cases: Commission v Italy (7/68), Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14).

cards.q: The Alcohol (Minimum Pricing) (Scotland) Act introduced a minimum retail price per unit of alcohol for all alcoholic drinks sold in Scotland. In a 2015 preliminary ruling the CJEU held that such rules could restrict the internal market, and that the national court must determine whether other, less restrictive measures could protect human health and life just as effectively while restricting trade within the Union less. (c) Assuming the scope applies, how could the measure infringe this fundamental freedom? Justify your answer on the facts. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It is a measure having equivalent effect to a quantitative restriction under Art 34 TFEU. It falls within the Dassonville formula and is not saved by Keck, because a fixed minimum retail price prevents the lower cost price of imported products from being reflected in their selling price. In fact, therefore, it affects imports differently from domestic products.
• It is not a quota, so not a quantitative restriction as such. It is a measure having equivalent effect (MEEQR). Dassonville (8/74): all trading rules of Member States capable of hindering intra-EU trade directly or indirectly, actually or potentially.
• Keck (C-267/91 and C-268/91): selling arrangements fall outside Art 34 only if they apply to all traders operating in the national territory and affect the marketing of domestic and imported products in the same manner, in law and in fact. A minimum price concerns how goods are sold, but by removing the competitive advantage of cheaper imports it does not affect them equally in fact and hinders their access to the market (Van Tiggele, 82/77; Scotch Whisky Association).
• Result: a restriction under Art 34 that must be justified (Art 36, public health) and proportionate. Mutual recognition (Cassis) is not the key here, because this is not a product requirement.
Codex: Arts 34, 36 TFEU · Cases: Dassonville (8/74), Keck and Mithouard (C-267/91 and C-268/91), Van Tiggele (82/77), Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14).

cards.q: The Alcohol (Minimum Pricing) (Scotland) Act introduced a minimum retail price per unit of alcohol for all alcoholic drinks sold in Scotland. In a 2015 preliminary ruling the CJEU held that such rules could restrict the internal market, and that the national court must determine whether other, less restrictive measures could protect human health and life just as effectively while restricting trade within the Union less. Scotland argues that minimum pricing protects public health, especially that of hazardous drinkers who buy cheap, strong alcohol. Critics say higher excise duties could also raise prices. Can minimum pricing be justified, and who must prove what? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It pursues a recognised aim, the protection of human health and life (Art 36 TFEU), but it is lawful only if proportionate: suitable, and not going beyond what is necessary. If a tax increase would be equally effective and less restrictive, minimum pricing is not justified. The Member State bears the burden of proof, and the national court decides.
• Art 36 grounds: public morality, public policy and public security; protection of the health and life of humans, animals or plants; national treasures; industrial and commercial property. Second sentence: no arbitrary discrimination and no disguised restriction on trade. Health ranks foremost among these interests, and Member States have discretion as to the level of protection they choose.
• Art 36 covers both distinctly and indistinctly applicable measures, so the Cassis mandatory requirements are not needed here.
• Suitability: minimum pricing targets cheap, strong drinks consumed by hazardous drinkers, so it is suitable, provided the aim is pursued in a consistent and systematic way.
• Necessity: higher excise duty may restrict trade less, because producers remain free to set their own prices. The Member State must show why taxation would be less effective, e.g. because it is less targeted.
• The national court assesses the evidence available when it rules. The Member State must show that the measure is appropriate and that no less restrictive alternative would be equally effective (Scotch Whisky Association, C-333/14).
• Aftermath: the UK Supreme Court upheld the law in 2017, and minimum pricing has applied since May 2018.
Codex: Arts 34, 36 TFEU; Art 5(4) TEU · Cases: Scotch Whisky Association (C-333/14), Cassis de Dijon (120/78).

cards.q: Luís Coentrão, a Portuguese lawyer, wants to emigrate with his family from Lisbon to Austria and open a law firm in Graz. His research shows that only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís is outraged and believes this violates Union law. (a) Which fundamental freedom could be affected? What indications are there in the facts? Where is this freedom regulated in the Treaties? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The freedom of establishment, Art 49 TFEU (within Arts 49–55). As a Portuguese national, and so a Union citizen, Luís wants to take up and pursue a self-employed activity in Austria permanently, through a fixed establishment of his own: a law firm.
• Indications in the facts: he emigrates with his family, which points to permanence and to stable and continuous participation in the economic life of another Member State (Gebhard, C-55/94; Factortame II, C-221/89). "Opening a law firm" is a self-employed activity with his own infrastructure. It is not employment, since there is no subordination (Lawrie-Blum, 66/85), so Art 45 does not apply. It is for an indefinite period, not temporary, so the freedom to provide services (Arts 56–57) does not apply; services are in any case residual (Art 57(1)).
• Personal scope and cross-border element: he is a national of a Member State (Art 49(1)) moving from Portugal to Austria.
• Content (Art 49(2)): establishment covers taking up and pursuing activities as a self-employed person and setting up undertakings under the conditions the host state lays down for its own nationals, i.e. national treatment.
• Secondary law to check first: Directive 98/5 (lawyers practising under their home title) and Directive 2005/36 (recognition of professional qualifications).
Codex: Arts 49, 51, 52, 53, 57 TFEU; Directive 98/5/EC; Directive 2005/36/EC · Cases: Reyners (2/74), Gebhard (C-55/94), Factortame II (C-221/89).

cards.q: Luís Coentrão, a Portuguese lawyer, wants to emigrate with his family from Lisbon to Austria and open a law firm in Graz. His research shows that only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís is outraged and believes this violates Union law. (b) Is this freedom actually infringed? Argue using the examination structure. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. The nationality requirement is direct discrimination. It is not covered by the official-authority exception (Art 51) or by any written ground of justification (Art 52), so it infringes Art 49 TFEU, which has direct effect (Reyners).
• (1) Scope: Art 49 applies (a Union national, self-employed, permanent, cross-border). No harmonising act permits nationality requirements. On the contrary, Directive 98/5 (Arts 2–3) entitles EU lawyers to practise permanently under their home title once registered in the host Member State.
• Exception (Art 51(1)): activities connected, even occasionally, with the exercise of official authority are excluded. A lawyer's activities, including advice and representation, even where representation is compulsory, are not official authority (Reyners, 2/74: a Belgian nationality requirement for the bar).
• (2) Restriction: a nationality condition is direct (open) discrimination, contrary to the national-treatment rule in Art 49(2). Keck-type reasoning is irrelevant, because the rule concerns access to the profession, not how it is exercised.
• (3) Justification: direct discrimination can be justified only on the written grounds in Art 52(1): public policy, public security or public health. These require a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental interest of society. Client protection is an unwritten overriding reason (Gebhard) and is not available for direct discrimination.
• (4) Proportionality: in any case, excluding all foreigners is not necessary, since checking qualifications would be less restrictive.
• Result: Art 49 is infringed. Luís can rely on it directly before Austrian authorities and courts, which must disapply the national rule (primacy).
• Correction of a common answer: Cassis de Dijon concerns goods and unwritten justifications; it cannot save a direct discrimination.
Codex: Arts 18, 49, 51, 52(1) TFEU; Directive 98/5/EC, Arts 2, 3 · Cases: Reyners (2/74), Gebhard (C-55/94).

cards.q: Luís Coentrão, a Portuguese lawyer, wants to emigrate with his family from Lisbon to Austria and open a law firm in Graz. His research shows that only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís is outraged and believes this violates Union law. (c) The Austrian Bar Association tells Luís that he can in principle open a law firm, but that before he is registered he must either work in Austria for three years or pass an aptitude test. His application for immediate registration is rejected. Luís now wants to bring an action for annulment before the General Court. What does he need to consider? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: The action would be inadmissible. Art 263 TFEU allows review only of acts of Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, and the Bar Association's refusal is a NATIONAL act. Luís must appeal against it before the competent Austrian courts. Those courts may, and at last instance must, refer questions on Art 49 TFEU and the lawyers' directives to the CJEU (Art 267).
• The General Court cannot annul national measures. Other options are a complaint to the Commission (Art 258) and Francovich damages. Whether the requirement is justified is a separate question of substance; this mark is for the procedural point.
Codex: Art 263(1), (4), Arts 258, 267 TFEU; Art 19(1)(2) TEU.

cards.q: Luís Coentrão, a Portuguese lawyer, wants to emigrate with his family from Lisbon to Austria and open a law firm in Graz. His research shows that only Austrian citizens may run a law firm in Austria. Luís is outraged and believes this violates Union law. The Austrian Bar Association tells him that, before he can be registered, he must either work in Austria for three years or pass an aptitude test, and it rejects his application for immediate registration. Assess the substance: is this requirement compatible with EU law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It depends on what Luís applies for. Registration under his Portuguese title ("advogado") must be granted on presentation of his home-state certificate (Directive 98/5, Art 3). But admission as an Austrian "Rechtsanwalt" may lawfully depend on three years of effective and regular practice in Austrian and EU law, or on an aptitude test (Directive 98/5, Art 10; Directive 2005/36, Art 14).
• Treaty test: qualification requirements that apply without distinction restrict establishment, but they can be justified by overriding reasons such as client protection and the proper administration of justice. Gebhard's four conditions: applied without discrimination, justified by imperative requirements in the general interest, suitable, and no more than necessary.
• The host Member State must take account of qualifications already obtained and compare them with its own requirements (Vlassopoulou, C-340/89; Morgenbesser, C-313/01).
• Directive 2005/36, Art 14(3): for professions requiring precise knowledge of national law, where advice on national law is an essential and constant part of the work, the host Member State may itself choose between an adaptation period and an aptitude test.
• Result: refusing immediate registration as a Rechtsanwalt is lawful. Refusing registration under his home title would breach Directive 98/5 and Art 49.
Codex: Arts 49, 53(1) TFEU; Directive 98/5/EC, Arts 2, 3, 10; Directive 2005/36/EC, Art 14 · Cases: Gebhard (C-55/94), Vlassopoulou (C-340/89), Morgenbesser (C-313/01).

cards.q: Dr Iwanow, a Russian citizen, travels from Moscow to Vienna on business, falls in love with the city and wants to live and work there. While viewing a flat in Vienna's 8th district, his estate agent tells him that, as a third-country national, he needs an official permit from the municipal authority under § 4 of the regional law on the acquisition of real estate by foreigners. (a) Which fundamental freedom could be affected in this case, and where is it regulated? Who is the addressee of this provision? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The free movement of capital, Art 63(1) TFEU (within Arts 63–66). It is addressed to the Member States, including their regions and municipalities (here the City and Land of Vienna). It protects everyone, whatever their nationality or residence, including third-country nationals.
• Acquisition of real estate by a non-resident is a capital movement. Annex I to Directive 88/361, heading II "investments in real estate", serves as an indicative list (Trummer and Mayer, C-222/97; Konle, C-302/97, on a Tyrolean land law).
• The other freedoms do not help: Arts 45, 49 and 56 protect only Union citizens (and, under Art 54, companies). As a Russian, Iwanow cannot rely on them for living or working.
• Correction of a common answer: the freedom is not limited to "EU citizens and people closely connected to them". Art 63 is the only freedom that extends to movements between Member States and third countries.
Codex: Arts 63(1), 64, 65 TFEU · Cases: Konle (C-302/97), Trummer and Mayer (C-222/97).

cards.q: Dr Iwanow, a Russian citizen, travels from Moscow to Vienna on business, falls in love with the city and wants to live and work there. While viewing a flat in Vienna's 8th district, his estate agent tells him that, as a third-country national, he needs an official permit from the municipal authority under § 4 of the regional law on the acquisition of real estate by foreigners. (b) Are third-country nationals in principle within the personal scope of this freedom? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Art 63(1) prohibits all restrictions on capital movements "between Member States and between Member States and third countries". Protection attaches to the transaction, not to the investor's nationality, so a Russian buying property in Vienna is covered, subject to the special exceptions in Arts 64–66.
Codex: Arts 63(1), 64–66 TFEU · Cases: Sanz de Lera (C-163/94), A (C-101/05).

cards.q: Dr Iwanow, a Russian citizen, travels from Moscow to Vienna on business, falls in love with the city and wants to live and work there. While viewing a flat in Vienna's 8th district, his estate agent tells him that, as a third-country national, he needs an official permit from the municipal authority under § 4 of the regional law on the acquisition of real estate by foreigners. (c) Name one activity related to real estate that falls within the scope of this freedom. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Buying real property (a flat, house or plot of land) in a Member State as a non-resident, i.e. an "investment in real estate" under heading II of Annex I to Directive 88/361. Other examples: securing a purchase with a mortgage from a bank in another state (Trummer and Mayer), or inheriting property.
• Correction of a common answer: Art 64(1) mentions "direct investment – including in real estate" only for the standstill exception for third countries. It does not define the scope of Art 63.
Codex: Arts 63(1), 64(1) TFEU; Directive 88/361, Annex I · Cases: Konle (C-302/97), Trummer and Mayer (C-222/97).

cards.q: Dr Iwanow, a Russian citizen, travels from Moscow to Vienna on business, falls in love with the city and wants to live and work there. While viewing a flat in Vienna's 8th district, his estate agent tells him that, as a third-country national, he needs an official permit from the municipal authority under § 4 of the regional law on the acquisition of real estate by foreigners. (d) Can one in principle rely directly on this fundamental freedom to derive rights? Justify your answer. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. Art 63(1) TFEU contains a clear, precise and unconditional prohibition that needs no implementing measures, so it has direct effect, also in relations with third countries (Sanz de Lera, C-163/94; A, C-101/05). The exceptions in Arts 64–65 are subject to judicial review and do not make it conditional.
Codex: Art 63(1) TFEU · Cases: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Sanz de Lera (C-163/94), A (C-101/05).

cards.q: Dr Iwanow, a Russian citizen, travels from Moscow to Vienna on business, falls in love with the city and wants to live and work there. While viewing a flat in Vienna's 8th district, his estate agent tells him that, as a third-country national, he needs an official permit from the municipal authority under § 4 of the regional law on the acquisition of real estate by foreigners. (e) Is the permit requirement under Austrian law permissible in this specific case? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Probably yes. The permit requirement restricts Art 63(1), but for a third-country national it can be covered by the standstill clause in Art 64(1) TFEU, which allows restrictions on "direct investment – including in real estate" that existed on 31 December 1993 to be kept in relation to third countries. Otherwise it would have to be justified (Art 65(1)(b) or an overriding reason) and be proportionate.
• Restriction: a prior permit for foreigners makes acquisition harder (Konle, C-302/97). Against EU and EEA citizens it would be unlawful, which is why Austrian land laws exempt them.
• Art 64(1) applies only to third countries. The rule must have existed on 31 December 1993, a date that also applies to Austria (Holböck, C-157/05), or a later rule must be substantially identical or less restrictive; a new approach is not covered (Konle). Austrian Länder had such laws before 1994, so the requirement is likely covered, if the purchase counts as "direct investment including in real estate" (debated).
• Otherwise: justification under Art 65(1)(b) (public policy or security) or an overriding reason (e.g. spatial planning), within Art 65(3) and proportionality. A permit based on objective criteria known in advance could pass; a blanket ban would not.
Codex: Arts 63(1), 64(1), 65(1)(b), 65(3) TFEU · Cases: Konle (C-302/97), Holböck (C-157/05), Reisch (C-515/99).

cards.q: German law requires fruit liqueurs to contain at least 25% alcohol. The French liqueur "Cassis de Dijon", lawfully produced and marketed in France with 15–20% alcohol, therefore cannot be sold in Germany. Germany argues that the rule applies equally to domestic and imported liqueurs and protects consumers and health. Assess this under the free movement of goods, and explain the principle of mutual recognition. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The rule is a measure having equivalent effect under Art 34 TFEU. It cannot be justified by the mandatory requirements invoked, because a less restrictive means (labelling) exists. Goods lawfully produced and marketed in one Member State must in principle be admitted in the others (mutual recognition; Cassis de Dijon, 120/78).
• Dassonville: product requirements that apply without distinction but can hinder trade are MEEQRs. Imported products have to be adapted, a "dual burden".
• Cassis "rule of reason": in the absence of harmonisation, obstacles resulting from differences between national laws must be accepted only in so far as they are necessary to satisfy mandatory requirements. The Court named the effectiveness of fiscal supervision, public health, the fairness of commercial transactions and consumer protection; the list is open (e.g. environmental protection).
• Application: the health argument fails, because lower-alcohol drinks are widely available and a high minimum does nothing for health. Consumers can be protected by labelling the alcohol content. The rule is therefore disproportionate.
• Mutual recognition: there is a presumption that a product lawfully marketed in one Member State may be sold in the others unless the host state proves a justification (now Reg (EU) 2019/515).
Codex: Arts 34, 36 TFEU; Reg (EU) 2019/515 · Cases: Cassis de Dijon (Rewe-Zentral, 120/78), Dassonville (8/74).

cards.q: Distinguish product requirements from selling arrangements (Keck) and apply the distinction to: (a) a French prohibition on reselling goods at a loss, which applies to all traders; (b) a national ban on advertising alcoholic drinks in magazines, which in practice makes it harder for new foreign products than for traditional domestic ones already familiar to consumers; (c) a rule requiring energy drinks to be sold in bottles of a specific shape. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) A selling arrangement outside Art 34 (Keck). (b) A selling arrangement that in fact affects imports more, so it falls within Art 34 (Gourmet). (c) A product requirement, and so a MEEQR (Cassis).
• Keck (C-267/91 and C-268/91, 1993): national rules restricting or prohibiting certain selling arrangements are not MEEQRs, provided they apply to all relevant traders operating in the national territory and affect the marketing of domestic and imported products in the same manner, in law and in fact. Product requirements (designation, form, size, weight, composition, presentation, labelling, packaging) remain MEEQRs, because they impose a dual burden.
• (a) Keck itself: resale at a loss concerns who sells, when and how, so it is outside Art 34.
• (b) Gourmet International (C-405/98): an alcohol advertising ban hits products from other Member States harder, because consumers already know the domestic ones. It is therefore a MEEQR, which can be justified on health grounds (Art 36) if proportionate. See also De Agostini (C-34/95).
• (c) Packaging or shape is a product requirement, so it is a MEEQR that needs justification (Cassis or Art 36) and must be proportionate.
• Later case law uses a market-access test for restrictions on use (Commission v Italy, trailers, C-110/05; Mickelsson and Roos, C-142/05).
Codex: Arts 34, 36 TFEU · Cases: Keck and Mithouard (C-267/91 and C-268/91), Gourmet International (C-405/98), Cassis de Dijon (120/78), Commission v Italy (C-110/05).

cards.q: Set out the general examination scheme for a fundamental freedom (goods, workers, establishment, services, capital), naming the relevant Treaty provisions and leading cases at each step. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) Scope, (2) restriction, (3) justification, (4) proportionality, preceded by a check of whether secondary law exhaustively harmonises the matter.
• (0) Secondary law first: where a field is exhaustively harmonised, the measure is judged only against the harmonising act. The Treaty freedoms still matter for that act's validity.
• (1) Scope, material: goods (Arts 28–37), workers (Art 45), establishment (Arts 49, 54), services (Arts 56–57, residual and temporary), capital (Art 63). Scope, personal: beneficiaries are Union nationals and companies; for goods, any product in free circulation; for capital, everyone. Addressees are the Member States (all public bodies) and exceptionally private parties (Walrave, Bosman, Angonese; collective action in Viking, C-438/05). There must be a cross-border element, not a purely internal situation. Exceptions to scope: public service (Art 45(4)) and official authority (Art 51).
• (2) Restriction: direct discrimination (nationality or origin); indirect discrimination (criteria mainly met by nationals, such as residence or language); or a non-discriminatory obstacle to market access (Dassonville 8/74, Cassis 120/78, Gebhard C-55/94, Säger C-76/90, Kraus C-19/92, Bosman C-415/93). For goods, Keck selling arrangements are excluded if they affect domestic and imported products equally in law and in fact.
• (3) Justification: written grounds (Arts 36, 45(3), 52(1), 62, 65(1)) are available for all restrictions. Unwritten overriding reasons in the public interest (Cassis mandatory requirements, Gebhard) are available as a rule only for measures that apply without distinction. Fundamental rights can also justify a restriction (Schmidberger, C-112/00).
• (4) Proportionality: a legitimate aim; suitability, including pursuit in a consistent and systematic way (Hartlauer, C-169/07); necessity (no less restrictive, equally effective means); appropriateness; and compatibility with the Charter (ERT, C-260/89). The burden of proof is on the Member State.
Codex: Arts 18, 26, 28–37, 45, 49–55, 56–62, 63–66 TFEU · Cases: Dassonville (8/74), Cassis de Dijon (120/78), Keck (C-267/91), Gebhard (C-55/94), Hartlauer (C-169/07), ERT (C-260/89).

cards.q: Deborah, a British national (the UK was then a Member State), wants to complete her paid preparatory service as a trainee teacher at a German state secondary school. She is refused admission because German law reserves the status of trainee civil servant to German nationals. Germany argues that teachers are in the "public service" under Article 45(4) TFEU. (a) Is Deborah a "worker"? (b) Does Article 45(4) apply? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes. She performs services for and under the direction of another person in return for remuneration (Lawrie-Blum, 66/85). (b) No. Art 45(4) is interpreted narrowly and covers only posts involving direct or indirect participation in powers conferred by public law and duties designed to safeguard the general interests of the state. Trainee teachers do not qualify.
• "Worker" is an autonomous EU concept and is interpreted broadly. It requires a genuine and effective activity that is not purely marginal and ancillary (Levin, 53/81), subordination and remuneration. A paid training period qualifies.
• Art 45(2) prohibits nationality discrimination in employment, remuneration and other working conditions; see also Reg 492/2011.
• Art 45(4) concerns access to posts only, not conditions once someone has been admitted (Sotgiu, 152/73). It is applied functionally to posts that presume a special relationship of allegiance to the state (Commission v Belgium, 149/79). Civil-servant status under national law is irrelevant.
• Result: the refusal is direct discrimination contrary to Art 45(2). It could be justified only under Art 45(3) (public policy, security or health), which does not apply here.
Codex: Art 45(1)–(4) TFEU; Reg 492/2011 · Cases: Lawrie-Blum (66/85), Levin (53/81), Sotgiu (152/73), Commission v Belgium (149/79).

cards.q: Distinguish the freedom to provide services from the freedom of establishment and from the free movement of workers. Apply the distinction to: (a) a German lawyer who, working from his Stuttgart office, regularly travels to Milan to represent clients but has no office there; (b) the same lawyer opening a permanent office in Milan; (c) an Austrian who travels to Italy to receive medical treatment. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Services (Arts 56–57). (b) Establishment (Art 49). (c) The passive freedom to receive services (Art 56; Luisi and Carbone).
• Workers (Art 45): employed activity under subordination. Establishment (Art 49): self-employed, with stable and continuous participation in the host state's economy through a fixed establishment for an indefinite period. Services (Arts 56–57): self-employed, temporary provision across borders for remuneration. Services are residual (Art 57(1)). Whether an activity is temporary depends on its duration, regularity, periodicity and continuity, and some infrastructure (an office, chambers) is allowed (Gebhard, C-55/94).
• (a) Temporary activity with no fixed base means services. The host state may not impose all the conditions it applies to establishment, and restrictions must be justified by overriding reasons and be proportionate (Säger, C-76/90). See also Directive 77/249 on lawyers' services.
• (b) A permanent office means establishment. Host-state rules apply in principle, subject to Art 49 (Gebhard).
• (c) Recipients of services are protected too (Luisi and Carbone, 286/82 and 26/83; for cross-border healthcare, Kohll, C-158/96, and Directive 2011/24).
Codex: Arts 45, 49, 56, 57, 62 TFEU · Cases: Gebhard (C-55/94), Säger (C-76/90), Luisi and Carbone (286/82 and 26/83), Kohll (C-158/96).

cards.q: Rudy, a French student in his fourth year at a Belgian university, supported himself during the first three years. He then applies for the Belgian "minimex" (minimum subsistence allowance), which Belgian students in the same situation receive. Belgium refuses because he is neither a Belgian national nor a worker. Can Rudy rely on EU primary law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. As a Union citizen lawfully resident in Belgium, he can rely on Art 18 TFEU together with Arts 20–21 TFEU. Refusing him a non-contributory benefit that Belgian nationals receive is direct discrimination on grounds of nationality (Grzelczyk, C-184/99), subject only to the limits in secondary law (Directive 2004/38).
• Art 20(1): every national of a Member State is a Union citizen, a status "destined to be the fundamental status of nationals of the Member States" (Grzelczyk). Arts 20(2)(a) and 21(1): the right to move and reside freely, subject to the limits and conditions in the Treaties and secondary law. For students, Directive 2004/38 requires sufficient resources and sickness insurance (Art 7(1)(c)).
• Art 18 prohibits any discrimination on grounds of nationality within the scope of the Treaties. Lawful residence as a Union citizen brings Rudy within that scope (Martínez Sala, C-85/96).
• Limits: the host state may conclude that a citizen who has become an unreasonable burden no longer meets the residence conditions, but not automatically. Under Art 24(2) of the Directive it may refuse social assistance during the first three months and maintenance aid for studies before permanent residence (five years). Economically inactive citizens who move only to obtain social assistance can be refused (Dano, C-333/13).
• Art 18 applies only where no specific freedom (Arts 45, 49, 56) applies.
Codex: Arts 18, 20, 21 TFEU; Directive 2004/38, Arts 7, 24 · Cases: Grzelczyk (C-184/99), Martínez Sala (C-85/96), Dano (C-333/13).

cards.q: EU competition rules aim to ensure that undertakings compete in the internal market on the basis of performance. (a) Is an intention to make a profit required for an entity to be an "undertaking" under competition law? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. An undertaking is any entity engaged in an economic activity, i.e. offering goods or services on a market, regardless of its legal status, how it is financed, or whether it seeks profit (Höfner and Elser, C-41/90, the German Federal Employment Office; MOTOE, C-49/07, a non-profit association).
• Not undertakings: bodies exercising public powers (Eurocontrol, C-364/92) or running solidarity-based social security schemes (Poucet and Pistre, C-159/91).
Codex: Arts 101, 102 TFEU · Cases: Höfner and Elser (C-41/90), MOTOE (C-49/07), Eurocontrol (C-364/92), Poucet and Pistre (C-159/91).

cards.q: EU competition rules aim to ensure that undertakings compete in the internal market on the basis of performance. (b) Name one example of a form of anti-competitive agreement under cartel law. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: For example, a horizontal agreement between competitors to fix selling prices (Art 101(1)(a) TFEU). Other examples: limiting production or markets (b), sharing markets or customers (c), discriminatory conditions (d), tying (e), or resale price maintenance in a vertical agreement.
• Art 101(1) catches agreements between undertakings, decisions by associations of undertakings and concerted practices that may affect trade between Member States and have as their object or effect the appreciable prevention, restriction or distortion of competition.
Codex: Art 101(1)(a)–(e) TFEU.

cards.q: EU competition rules aim to ensure that undertakings compete in the internal market on the basis of performance. (c) A national court is dealing with a cartel case, and shortly afterwards the European Commission opens proceedings on the same infringement. What must the court consider to avoid conflicting decisions? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under Art 16(1) of Reg 1/2003, the national court must avoid any decision that would conflict with a decision the Commission is contemplating in proceedings it has opened. It may therefore stay its own proceedings until the Commission decides. It may never rule against a Commission decision already adopted (Masterfoods, C-344/98).
• It may ask the Commission for information or for its opinion (Art 15(1)) and may refer to the CJEU under Art 267. If the Commission decision is challenged before the EU courts, the national court should stay its proceedings until they rule (Masterfoods).
Codex: Arts 15, 16(1) Reg 1/2003; Art 4(3) TEU; Art 267 TFEU · Case: Masterfoods (C-344/98).

cards.q: EU competition rules aim to ensure that undertakings compete in the internal market on the basis of performance. (d) Name two legal consequences of an established infringement of the cartel prohibition. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) The prohibited agreement or clause is automatically void (Art 101(2) TFEU). (2) The Commission can impose fines of up to 10% of the undertaking's total worldwide turnover in the preceding business year (Art 23(2) Reg 1/2003). Further consequences: damages claims by those harmed, orders to end the infringement, and periodic penalty payments.
• Art 101(2): void ex tunc and for everyone, but only the prohibited clauses if they can be severed (Société Technique Minière, 56/65). National contract law governs the rest of the contract.
• Fines depend on the gravity and duration of the infringement (Art 23(3)), with a leniency programme for cartel members who come forward. National competition authorities can also impose fines (Art 5 Reg 1/2003).
• The Commission can order the infringement to end, with behavioural or structural remedies (Art 7), and impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily turnover (Art 24).
• Private enforcement: anyone harmed can claim full compensation (Courage; Manfredi; Directive 2014/104).
Codex: Art 101(1)–(2) TFEU; Reg 1/2003, Arts 5, 7, 23, 24; Directive 2014/104 · Cases: Société Technique Minière (56/65), Courage v Crehan (C-453/99).

cards.q: Two car manufacturers agree to develop an electric-vehicle battery technology jointly and to share the patents. A third company, which holds 70% of the EU market for charging software, refuses to license its interface to competitors and grants loyalty rebates. Explain Article 101(3) TFEU and Article 102 TFEU and apply them in outline. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The research and development agreement may be exempted under Art 101(3) if its four conditions are met. The software company, with 70% of the market, is presumably dominant and may be abusing that position under Art 102 by refusing access and granting loyalty rebates. Art 102 has no exemption, only objective justification.
• Art 101(3): an agreement is exempt if it (1) contributes to improving production or distribution or to technical or economic progress, (2) allows consumers a fair share of the benefit, (3) imposes only indispensable restrictions, and (4) does not allow competition to be eliminated for a substantial part of the products. This is a directly applicable legal exception, so no prior decision is needed (Art 1(2) Reg 1/2003). The undertakings bear the burden of proof (Art 2). Block exemptions exist, e.g. for R&D agreements (Reg 2023/1066).
• Art 102: (1) one or more undertakings; (2) a dominant position on the relevant product and geographic market, i.e. economic strength that allows it to act to an appreciable extent independently of competitors, customers and consumers (United Brands, 27/76). A market share above 50% raises a presumption of dominance (AKZO, C-62/86). (3) Abuse, either exploitative or exclusionary; see the examples in Art 102(a)–(d). A refusal to license can be abusive in exceptional circumstances (Microsoft, T-201/04), and loyalty rebates can be too (Hoffmann-La Roche, 85/76; Intel, C-413/14 P, which requires an effects analysis). (4) An effect on trade between Member States.
• Dominance itself is not prohibited. Only its abuse is.
Codex: Art 101(1), (3), Art 102 TFEU; Reg 1/2003, Arts 1, 2 · Cases: United Brands (27/76), Hoffmann-La Roche (85/76), AKZO (C-62/86), Microsoft (T-201/04), Intel (C-413/14 P).

cards.q: Mr Crehan, a pub tenant, was bound by a beer-tie clause in his lease with the pub company Courage. It obliged him to buy beer only from Courage, at prices higher than those charged to free houses, and his pub failed. When Courage sued him for unpaid deliveries, he counterclaimed damages, arguing that the tie was an agreement contrary to Article 101 TFEU. English law barred a party to an illegal contract from claiming damages from the other party. (a) Can a party to an anti-competitive agreement claim damages? (b) What does Directive 2014/104 add? (3 points)
cards.a:
