Short answer: (a) Yes. Any individual, even a party to the agreement, must be able to claim damages for loss caused by an agreement contrary to Art 101. National law may refuse this only to a party that bears significant responsibility for the distortion of competition (Courage v Crehan, C-453/99). (b) The Damages Directive harmonises key rules for such claims.
• Basis: Art 101(1) has direct effect between private parties, and effet utile requires a damages remedy. The prohibition's full effectiveness would be at risk if nobody could claim damages, and such claims strengthen enforcement (Courage; Manfredi, C-295/04: any individual can claim actual loss, loss of profit and interest).
• Limits: procedural autonomy, subject to equivalence and effectiveness; no unjust enrichment. A party with significant responsibility may be barred, but Crehan, as a weak tenant, was not in that position.
• Directive 2014/104: right to full compensation (Art 3); disclosure of evidence (Arts 5–8); a final infringement decision of a national competition authority binds courts of the same Member State (Art 9); limitation period of at least five years (Art 10); joint and several liability (Art 11); rules on passing-on and indirect purchasers (Arts 12–14); a rebuttable presumption that cartels cause harm (Art 17(2)). Austria implemented it in the Kartellgesetz (§§ 37a ff.).
Codex: Art 101 TFEU; Directive 2014/104/EU · Cases: Courage v Crehan (C-453/99), Manfredi (C-295/04 to C-298/04), BRT v SABAM (127/73).

cards.q: In London only licensed black cabs may use bus lanes, while pre-booked minicabs may not. Black cabs may be hailed in the street and are subject to strict licensing, fixed fares and an obligation to accept hires. Minicab operator Maxitaxi argues that the bus-lane rule is unlawful state aid in favour of black cabs. Explain the elements of state aid under Article 107(1) TFEU, the procedure under Article 108 TFEU and the role of national courts, and assess the bus-lane rule in outline. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: State aid requires (1) an intervention by the state or through state resources, (2) an economic advantage, (3) selectivity, (4) a distortion of competition and (5) an effect on trade between Member States. Only the Commission decides whether aid is compatible (Arts 107(2)–(3), 108), while national courts enforce the standstill obligation (Art 108(3)). The bus-lane rule probably involves neither state resources nor selectivity (Eventech, C-518/13).
• Art 107(1): the elements are cumulative. Art 107(2): categories of aid compatible by law (e.g. aid for natural disasters). Art 107(3): aid that may be declared compatible (regional, sectoral, important projects of common European interest).
• Art 108(3): new aid must be notified and may not be granted until the Commission decides. This standstill has direct effect, so national courts must draw the consequences, e.g. recovery of aid granted unlawfully (SFEI, C-39/94; CELF, C-199/06). Only the Commission assesses compatibility.
• Assessment: access to bus lanes transfers no state resources and involves no revenue forgone. Selectivity requires a comparison between undertakings in a comparable legal and factual situation. Black cabs (hailing, strict licensing, obligation to accept hires, fixed fares, wheelchair access) and minicabs (pre-booked only) are not comparable. So there is probably no aid, which the national court must verify.
Codex: Art 107(1)–(3), Art 108(2)–(3) TFEU · Cases: Eventech (C-518/13), SFEI (C-39/94), CELF (C-199/06), Altmark (C-280/00).

cards.q: The euro crisis was tackled, among other things, through stricter financial market regulation, e.g. Directive 2010/76/EU as a substantive measure. Name one other measure or instrument created to tackle the euro crisis. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: For example, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM, 2012), a permanent intergovernmental rescue fund of the euro-area states, backed by the new Art 136(3) TFEU and upheld in Pringle (C-370/12). Alternatives: EFSF/EFSM (2010); the "six-pack" and "two-pack"; the Fiscal Compact (TSCG, 2012); the European Semester; the Banking Union (SSM, SRM); the ECB's OMT programme (Gauweiler, C-62/14).
• Correction of a common answer: the Eurogroup is not a crisis measure. It existed before the crisis, as an informal body since 1998, now in Protocol No 14.
Codex: Arts 121, 125, 126, 136(3) TFEU · Cases: Pringle (C-370/12), Gauweiler (C-62/14).

cards.q: A directive adopted under Article 114 TFEU harmonises national rules on the marketing and use of certain dangerous substances and mixtures, including a maximum concentration for the chemical "PCP". Years later a study published in Spain concludes that the permitted concentration may be set too high. Spain wants to raise its level of protection and introduce new rules that depart from the harmonised EU standard. Under which conditions is this permitted? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: For NEW national provisions, Art 114(5) TFEU applies. They must be based on new scientific evidence relating to the protection of the environment or the working environment, on grounds of a problem specific to Spain that arose after the harmonising measure was adopted. They must be notified to the Commission, which must approve them (Art 114(6)).
• Distinguish Art 114(4), which concerns MAINTAINING existing national provisions on grounds of the major needs in Art 36 or of environmental or working-environment protection. No new evidence is needed there. Public health can be invoked only under Art 114(4), not under Art 114(5).
• The Commission approves or rejects within six months, extendable by up to six more, after checking that the rules are neither arbitrary discrimination nor a disguised restriction on trade and are no obstacle to the internal market. If it does not decide in time, the rules are deemed approved (Art 114(6)). Spain may not apply them before approval (Kortas, C-319/97). A "specific problem" is interpreted strictly (Land Oberösterreich, C-439/05 P: an Austrian ban on GMOs was rejected).
• If Spain misuses these powers, the Commission can go directly to the Court (Art 114(9)).
Codex: Arts 36, 114(4)–(9) TFEU · Cases: Kortas (C-319/97), Land Oberösterreich (C-439/05 P).
